media.title: Unit Picker

tool_config.idea: Choose cm or m for a length by comparing the number with the size of the thing: a pencil of 17 is 17 cm, because 17 m would be longer than a classroom. This is the free first try of the chapter, so it asks and shows; the videos that follow name the rule.
tool_config.title: Unit Picker
tool_config.screen: The long cloth table of the village weaving centre, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation, with a measuring tape running along the top of the wall. A picture card of a thing (a pencil, a classroom door, a school bus, a postage stamp, a handkerchief) stands on the table as the largest object on screen, with a number tag beside it, for example 17. Under the card are two unit tags, cm and m, to drag onto the number tag. A tape strip along the wall draws the length as a bar for the chosen unit, with a 1 m mark and a 1 cm mark always shown, so a wrong unit makes the bar run far past the picture or shrink to a dot. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag the cm tag or the m tag onto the number tag; tap the tag again to take it off; in the rule card, drag the unit cards cm and m into two gaps; answer tags for the book's questions; Check, Hint, Retry (takes the tag off this card), Reset (returns all cards), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the number with its unit under the picture, the bar on the wall tape, and a card number out of 7.
feedback: A tag dropped on a number draws a bar on the wall tape. If the bar runs far past the picture, the tool says, for example: 17 m is longer than a classroom, but a pencil is small. Try the other tag.
If the bar shrinks to a dot, the tool says, for example: 2 cm is a tiny length, but a door is tall. Try the other tag.
A tag that fits locks in with a soft chime and the bar turns green, with the words: 17 cm fits the pencil.
In the book's questions the bar is drawn after the student has chosen a unit, and the tool says whether the length is sensible, in the same plain words.
A wrong rule card slides back with a clue such as: Think of a pencil. Is it short or long?
tool_config.done_when: All four picture cards have the right tag, the rule is finished, and all six lengths of Let Us Find have a unit.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Unit Picker
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S1.T1.C2.2D1
- Tool type: Exploration (the free first try right after the story video)
- Textbook source: Far and Near, the opening table "Let Us Find" (India Gate 42, handkerchief 40, well 50, mobile phone 13, elephant's trunk 2, two buttons on a shirt 5; choose m or cm) and the story of Shikha and Sonu. Practice values added: 9, 7, 11, 3 (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that the same number means very different lengths in cm and in m, and picks the unit that gives a sensible length for the thing.
- Out of scope: changing between m and cm, mm and km, comparing two lengths, sums with lengths.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A pale wooden table top in front of a cream wall (photo). Flat-drawn Shikha at the left holds the end of a yellow tape marked "cm"; flat-drawn Sonu at the right holds the end of a blue tape marked "m". In the middle stands the first picture card: a photo cut-out of a crayon in Shikha's open hand, about 40% of the stage width, with a big number tag "9" and an empty round slot after it: "9 [ ]". Under it lie a yellow "cm" tag and a blue "m" tag. A wall tape runs along the bottom of the stage.
- Instruction line: "Drop a unit tag on the number 9."
- The child is invited to drag a tag onto the slot.
2. Scene and Objects
- Picture card: one real thing as a photo cut-out at true size on the card's own tape scale, filling about 60% of the stage width (tall things 60% of the height). Shikha holds small things in her hand (crayon, stamp, eraser, key, button) and stands beside long things (wall, bus, tree, ground, pool) so the size can be felt.
- Number tag: a large rounded tag with the number and one slot. Unit tags "cm" and "m", each as wide as a thumb.
- Wall tape: a code-drawn pale yellow tape, 90% of the stage width, left end 0, drawn at the card's scale. In Activities 1 and 2 a short tick "1 cm" and a long tick "1 m" stand at its left end; a tick too far away shows as an arrow off the right edge, a tick too small as a dot.
- Bar: drawn only after Check, from the left end, as long as the number in the chosen unit; too long runs off the right edge, too short is a dot.
- Goal chip at the top left, for example "Crayon: 9 ?". Progress pills: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, star, star.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag a tag onto the slot (or tap the tag, then the slot). A second tag replaces the first. Tapping the tag in the slot takes it off (Undo).
- Check draws the bar and says whether the length fits. With an empty slot it only says "Drop a tag on the number first." and the slot pulses.
- Bottom buttons: Hint, Check (becomes Next when done), Reset. Retry is free.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Drop a unit tag on the number 9." Chip: "Crayon: 9 ?". Setup: crayon card, reference ticks shown. Guess: the child drops the tag they think fits before any bar is drawn. Result: with cm the bar is as long as the crayon and turns green: "A crayon fits in a hand: 9 cm. 9 m would run far past it." A chip "What if 9 m?" then pulses and draws the other bar faded. Help: guided.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Drop a unit tag on the number 7." Chip: "Classroom wall: 7 ?". Setup: a classroom wall with Shikha beside it, ticks shown. Guess: tag first. Result: "A classroom wall is long: 7 m. 7 cm is shorter than the crayon." Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Drop a unit tag on the number 11." Chip: "School bus: 11 ?". Setup: a school bus, no ticks. Guess: tag first. Result: "A school bus is long: 11 m. 11 cm is only about as long as a crayon." Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Drop a unit tag on the number 3." Chip: "Postage stamp: 3 ?". Setup: a stamp in Shikha's hand, no ticks. Guess: tag first. Result: "A stamp is tiny: 3 cm. 3 m is longer than a door." Help: independent.
- Activity 5 (independent). Goal line: "Drag each picture to the cm basket or the m basket." Chip: "Sort 6 pictures". Setup: baskets "cm" and "m"; six photo chips without numbers: eraser, key, button, tall tree, football ground, swimming pool. Guess: first the child taps how many go in the cm basket: "2", "3" or "4". Result: right chips stay green; the strip says "3 small things in the cm basket and 3 long things in the m basket." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1 (the book's question, parts a to c). Goal line: "Identify the appropriate units for measuring each of the following." Chip: "Pick m or cm for 3 things". Setup: three picture rows with a slot each: "Height of India Gate: 42 [ ]", "Length of a handkerchief: 40 [ ]", "Depth of a well: 50 [ ]", each with a "cm" and an "m" tag. Guess: the child fills all three slots, then Check. Result: right rows turn green and draw their bars: "42 m, 40 cm and 50 m. India Gate and a well are big; a handkerchief fits in a hand." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2 (parts d to f). Same layout: "Length of a mobile phone: 13 [ ]", "Length of an elephant's trunk: 2 [ ]", "Distance between two buttons on a shirt: 5 [ ]". Result: "13 cm, 2 m and 5 cm. A phone fits in a hand; a trunk is longer than a child's arm; two buttons are close together." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Seeing both bars on one number, the child notices that 9 cm and 9 m are the same number but lengths far apart, so the number alone does not give the length. They compare the bar with the thing and ask "how big is this thing?" before choosing a unit.
- Rules in the child's words: small things that fit in a hand are measured in cm; things as long as a room or longer are measured in m; the unit matters as much as the number.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the slot or row turns green and the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick, Next unlocks and the strip shows the result line. Confetti only on the end screen.
- Wrong (every case): red strip, a small shake of the tag and bar, and ONE friendly line; no score; the child tries again at once.
- m on a small thing -> "9 m is much too long for a crayon: a crayon fits in a hand. Look at the bar running past it." The picture and the long bar pulse (each card uses its own number and thing).
- cm on a long thing -> "11 cm is only about as long as a crayon, but a bus is long. Look at the tiny bar." The tiny bar pulses. Well: "50 cm is only up to your knee, but a well is deep." Trunk: "2 cm is about as wide as a thumb, but a trunk is long." India Gate: "42 cm is only as long as your arm, but India Gate is a very tall building."
- Empty slot on Check -> "Drop a tag on the number first." The slot pulses (no red).
- Sort: a long thing in the cm basket -> "A football ground is much longer than a hand. Try the other basket." The chip slides back.
- Hints (3 levels, one per press, reset for each activity): (1) "How big is the thing? Could you hold it in your hand, or is it as long as a room?" (2) both bars are drawn faded and Shikha's hand or standing figure glows beside the thing; (3) the wrong tag fades, the right tag glows: "A thing you can hold is measured in cm. A thing as long as a room or longer is measured in m. Which is this?" In a Star Challenge the hint works on the first row that is not green.
- Edge cases: one tag is always right for a card; a tag dropped outside the slot slides back; a sort chip can be moved between baskets any number of times.
7. Ending
- Star Challenge 1 is done when 42 m, 40 cm and 50 m are green; Star Challenge 2 when 13 cm, 2 m and 5 cm are green.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "A number needs a unit." "Small things that fit in a hand are measured in cm." "Things as long as a room or longer are measured in m." Think and talk: "Shikha and Sonu measure the same sari with different tapes. Why can they read different numbers?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Photo cut-outs (transparent, true proportions): crayon, classroom wall, school bus, postage stamp, eraser, key, button, tall tree, football ground, swimming pool, India Gate, folded handkerchief, well, mobile phone, elephant with trunk, shirt with two buttons. Photo of the table top and cream wall.
- Flat drawings: Shikha (hand pose and standing pose), Sonu, the yellow "cm" and blue "m" tape ends. Code-drawn: tape with ticks, bars, baskets.
- Language: simple English; every number has its unit beside it.

Worked example: Shikha measures a pencil and Sonu measures a classroom wall (practice values). The pencil is 17 long and the wall is 8 long. Write cm or m for each.
1. The pencil fits in a hand, so it is short. Its unit is cm: 17 cm.
2. The classroom wall is longer than a child, so it is long. Its unit is m: 8 m.
3. Check the pencil: 17 m would be longer than a classroom, so 17 cm is the sensible length.
4. Check the wall: 8 cm would be shorter than the pencil, so 8 m is the sensible length.
Answer: The pencil is 17 cm and the wall is 8 m, because the pencil is short and the wall is long

content.text:
1. Predict first: Shikha's tape says 300 and Sonu's tape says 3 for the same stole. Can both numbers be right?
2. Yes. The two tapes use different units. 1 m is the same length as 100 cm, so one length has two names.
3. A double number line shows both names. The top line is in m, the bottom line is in cm, and from the top line to the bottom line every number is multiplied by 100.
4. To change m to cm, multiply by 100: 3 m = 3 × 100 = 300 cm.
5. To change cm to m and cm, take out the hundreds: 450 cm = 400 cm + 50 cm = 4 m 50 cm, because 400 ÷ 100 = 4.
6. A part bigger than 100 cm is allowed too: 3 m 130 cm = 300 cm + 130 cm = 430 cm.
7. Rule: 1 m = 100 cm, so multiply by 100 to change m to cm.

1. The top line is in cm and the bottom line is in m. The arrow $\times 100$ says that m become cm when you multiply by $100$.

4. $500\text{ cm}$ is $500 \div 100 = 5\text{ m}$, so the next blank is $5\text{ m}$.
5. $700\text{ cm}$ is $700 \div 100 = 7\text{ m}$, so the last blank is $7\text{ m}$.
[Image: Different Units but Same Measure: Ans1: solution]
6. Check: $4 \times 100 = 400$, $5 \times 100 = 500$ and $7 \times 100 = 700$.
Answer: Top line: $200\text{ cm}$. Bottom line: $4\text{ m}$, $5\text{ m}$, $7\text{ m}$
[Image: Different Units but Same Measure: Ans1: solution (continued)]

media.title: Length Bars

tool_config.idea: Compare two lengths given in different units by changing both to one unit, and read the difference as the gap between two bars on one tape. A doubled bar helps find the length that doubles to a given length.
tool_config.title: Length Bars
tool_config.screen: The weaving centre's long wall tape in cm, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation, with rods and lengths of cloth hung along it. Two bars sit on one tape, drawn to scale, and they are the largest things on screen; each bar has a length card in its own units, for example 4 m 3 cm. A Change to cm button under each card shows the working, for example 4 × 100 + 3 = 403, and the card turns into cm. A sign box between the bars takes the signs <, = and >. A gap marker appears between the ends of the bars and shows the difference when both are in cm. A Double button stretches a bar to twice its length. In the statue stage the six statues of your maths book stand as bars on one base line (182 m, 128 m, 108 m, 93 m, 91 m and 38 m), and tapping two statues puts their bars side by side with the gap. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type with progress dots under it. Controls: Change to cm on each card; drag a sign into the sign box; tap two statues; Double; type an answer into a box; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the sign and the conversion of this card), Reset (restores all bars), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: each length in its own units and in cm, the gap in cm, and a card number out of 7.
feedback: Change to cm shows the working on the card, for example 4 × 100 + 3 = 403, and the bar redraws in cm. If the two lengths are still in different units, the tool says: Change both to the same unit first.
A sign dropped in the sign box is checked against the two numbers in cm and the tool says why, for example: 403 is less than 430, so the sign is <.
The gap marker shows the difference in cm only when both bars are in cm, and the tool says: The difference is the longer bar minus the shorter bar.
The Double button stretches a bar, and a bar of the same length lights up in green; if none matches, the tool says: Halve the long bar to find the short one.
In the statue stage, two tapped statues show their heights side by side and the gap, and the tool says whether the gap is the least or the largest only after the student has tried the pairs.
tool_config.done_when: All five practice cards are solved, the five rod comparisons have signs, and the four statue questions are answered.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): compare 4 m 3 cm and 430 cm. Change both to cm and drop a sign. Answer: 4 m 3 cm = 4 × 100 + 3 = 403 cm, and 403 < 430, so 4 m 3 cm < 430 cm.
Card 2 (practice values): compare 3 m 20 cm and 300 cm + 20 cm. Answer: 3 m 20 cm = 320 cm and 300 cm + 20 cm = 320 cm, so they are equal.
Card 3 (practice values): find the gap between 3 m 45 cm and 290 cm. Answer: 3 m 45 cm = 345 cm and 345 − 290 = 55 cm.
Card 4 (practice values): double a bar of 85 cm and find which of the bars 60 cm, 170 cm and 255 cm is the same length as the doubled bar. Answer: 85 × 2 = 170 cm, so the bar of 170 cm.

Card 5 (practice values): put three bars in order from the shortest to the longest after changing them to cm: 2 m 5 cm, 190 cm and 2 m 50 cm. Answer: 2 m 5 cm = 205 cm and 2 m 50 cm = 250 cm, so the order is 190 cm, 2 m 5 cm, 2 m 50 cm.

Challenge: 'Ritika is comparing the lengths of different rods. Compare them using <, =, > signs.' (a) 456 cm and 5 m; (b) 55 cm + 200 cm and 200 cm + 54 cm; (c) 6 m 5 cm and 6 m 50 cm; (d) 2 m 150 cm and 3 m 50 cm; (e) 238 cm and 138 cm + 1 m. Answer: (a) <; (b) >; (c) <; (d) =; (e) =.

Challenge: the world's tallest statues, with the heights 182 m, 128 m, 108 m, 93 m, 91 m and 38 m: (a) the difference between the height of the tallest statue and the Statue of Liberty; (b) the statues whose heights have the least difference; (c) the statues whose heights have the largest difference; (d) the statue whose height doubled is the height of the Statue of Unity. Answer: (a) 182 − 93 = 89 m; (b) the Statue of Liberty and The Motherland Calls, 2 m; (c) the Statue of Unity and Christ the Redeemer, 144 m; (d) The Motherland Calls, 91 m.

hint_ladder.text: Are the two lengths in the same unit? What must you do before you compare them?
Change both to cm, the smaller unit. 1 m is how many cm?
Change the m by multiplying by 100 and add the cm that are left. Then compare the two numbers.
The tool shows both lengths in cm. Compare the two numbers: the bigger number is the longer length.

Challenge: the world's tallest statues, with the heights 182 m, 128 m, 108 m, 93 m, 91 m and 38 m: (a) the difference between the height of the tallest statue and the Statue of Liberty; (b) the statues whose heights have the least difference; (c) the statues whose heights have the largest difference; (d) the statue whose height doubled is the height of the Statue of Unity. Answer: (a) 182 − 93 = 89 m; (b) the Statue of Liberty and The Motherland Calls, 2 m; (c) the Statue of Unity and Christ the Redeemer, 144 m; (d) The Motherland Calls, 91 m.

media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Length Bars
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S5.T5.C14.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Far and Near, "Let Us Compare": Ritika's five rod comparisons and the six tallest statues, parts (a) to (d). Practice values added: 4 m 3 cm, 430 cm, 3 m 20 cm, 3 m 45 cm, 290 cm, 85 cm (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student compares two lengths given in different units by changing both to the same unit, finds how much longer one is, and finds the length that doubles to a given length.
- Out of scope: km and mm, adding or subtracting lengths in columns, multiplying by numbers other than 2.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- Ritika's rod rack: a photo of a pegboard workshop wall with a long cm tape across it. Two thick painted rods hang under the tape, drawn to scale; a cloth flap hides the right end of each. Cards hang from them: "4 m 3 cm" on the left rod, "430 cm" on the right. An empty round sign box sits between the rods.
- Instruction line: "Change both lengths to cm, then drop a sign."
- The child is invited to tap "Change to cm" first.
2. Scene and Objects
- Tape: code-drawn cm tape, scale set per card so the longer rod fills about 85% of the stage width; bold ticks every 100 cm.
- Rods: two bars as thick as a thumb, one blue, one orange. Under each card a button "Change to cm"; a card already in cm shows a tick; a card with a sum, such as "55 cm + 200 cm", adds it when tapped.
- Sign box with chips "<", "=", ">" under it. Guess chips under the tape: "Left is longer", "Right is longer", "Same".
- Gap bracket: after Check, a dashed bracket between the rod ends shows the gap in cm, with a magnifying circle if it is under 3 cm on screen.
- Statue stage (Star Challenge 2): sunny hill and sky; six statue cut-outs on one base line at true relative height, with name tags: Statue of Unity 182 m, Spring Temple Buddha 128 m, Guanyin of Nanshan 108 m, Statue of Liberty 93 m, The Motherland Calls 91 m, Christ the Redeemer 38 m.
- Goal chip at the top left, for example "4 m 3 cm ? 430 cm". Pills: 1, 2, 3, 4, star, star.
3. Main Interaction
- Tap a guess chip first. Tap "Change to cm": three number chips pop up and the child taps one; the right chip turns the card into cm and shows the working; a wrong chip shakes. Drag a sign chip into the box (a second replaces the first). Tap two statues to compare them. "Double" stretches a rod to twice its length.
- Check lifts the flaps. Bottom buttons: Hint, Check (becomes Next when done), Reset. Undo is a small back arrow on the stage; retry is free.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Change both lengths to cm, then drop a sign." Chip: "4 m 3 cm ? 430 cm". Setup: rods "4 m 3 cm" and "430 cm". Guess: a guess chip. The child picks "403 cm" (others "43 cm", "430 cm"; the working "4 × 100 + 3" shows), drops a sign, presses Check. Result: the flaps lift: "4 m 3 cm is 4 × 100 + 3 = 403 cm, and 403 is less than 430, so 4 m 3 cm < 430 cm." Help: guided.
- Activity 2 (guided). Same goal line. Chip: "3 m 20 cm ? 300 cm + 20 cm". Setup: rods "3 m 20 cm" and "300 cm + 20 cm". Guess: a guess chip. Chips "320 cm", "50 cm", "3,020 cm"; the child taps the right card to add, drops a sign, Check. Result: both rods end together: "3 m 20 cm is 3 × 100 + 20 = 320 cm, and 300 cm + 20 cm = 320 cm, so the sign is =." Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "How much longer is the longer rod?" Chip: "Gap: ? cm". Setup: "3 m 45 cm" and "290 cm". Guess: tap the rod they think is longer. Chips "345 cm", "3,045 cm", "75 cm" for the left card, then the gap "55 cm", "45 cm" or "635 cm", Check. Result: "3 m 45 cm is 3 × 100 + 45 = 345 cm. The gap is 345 − 290 = 55 cm." Help: independent, no working shown.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Double the rod and find the rod of the same length." Chip: "Double of 85 cm: ?". Setup: a rod of 85 cm and rods "60 cm", "170 cm", "255 cm". Guess: tap the rod they think will match. Double stretches the 85 cm rod; the child taps the rod that ends at the same place, Check. Result: "85 × 2 = 170 cm, so the 170 cm rod is the same length." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1 (the book's question). Goal line: "Ritika is comparing the lengths of different rods. Compare them using <, =, > signs." Chip: "Compare 5 pairs". Five tabs: (a) "456 cm" and "5 m"; (b) "55 cm + 200 cm" and "200 cm + 54 cm"; (c) "6 m 5 cm" and "6 m 50 cm"; (d) "2 m 150 cm" and "3 m 50 cm"; (e) "238 cm" and "138 cm + 1 m". Each is worked like Activity 1, guess chip first. Change to cm chips: the right number, a number made by joining digits or taking 1 m as 10 cm, and one more wrong number; the right numbers are 500 cm for 5 m, 605 cm, 650 cm, 350 cm, 350 cm and 100 cm for 1 m. Answers: (a) <, (b) >, (c) <, (d) =, (e) =. Result for (c): "6 m 5 cm is 605 cm and 6 m 50 cm is 650 cm, so 6 m 5 cm < 6 m 50 cm." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2 (the book's question, parts a to d). Goal line: "Look at the picture of some of the world's tallest statues." Chip: "4 questions". Four tabs with the book's wording: (a) "What is the difference between the height of the tallest statue in the world and the Statue of Liberty?" The child taps the two statues, then picks "89 m", "99 m" or "275 m". (b) "Identify the statues whose heights have the least difference." The child taps two statues, the gap shows on a dashed bracket, other pairs may be tried, Check commits. (c) "Identify the statues whose heights have the largest difference." Same way. (d) "The height of which statue will be equal to the height of the Statue of Unity, if it is doubled?" The child taps a statue and Double: a dashed copy twice as tall appears; Check on the statue that reaches exactly the top. Guess: the first tap. Results: (a) "182 − 93 = 89 m"; (b) the Statue of Liberty and The Motherland Calls, "93 − 91 = 2 m"; (c) the Statue of Unity and Christ the Redeemer, "182 − 38 = 144 m"; (d) The Motherland Calls, "91 × 2 = 182 m". Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- The flaps make the child decide with numbers; when they lift, the cm numbers give the true order. The gap bracket shows the difference as how far the longer rod passes the shorter. A doubled rod meeting another shows that the length that doubles to 182 is half of 182.
- Rules in the child's words: change both to the same unit, the smaller one, then compare; the difference is the longer minus the shorter.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the chip or sign turns green, the flaps lift, the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick and Next unlocks. Confetti only on the end screen.
- Wrong (every case): red strip, a small shake, ONE friendly line; no score; try again at once.
- Sign dropped while a length is still in m and cm -> "The two lengths are in different units. Tap Change to cm on both first." The Change buttons pulse.
- Picks the card with the bigger unit as longer -> "m is a bigger unit, but that does not make the length longer. Change both to cm first." Both cards pulse.
- Joins digits or takes 1 m as 10 cm (a chip like "43 cm") -> "1 m is 100 cm, and 3 cm is only 3 cm. Write 4 m 3 cm as 4 × 100 + 3." The m part pulses.
- Wrong sign after both are in cm -> "Look at the two cm numbers, 403 and 430. Which is bigger? The longer rod has the bigger number." The two numbers pulse (each card uses its own).
- Gap "45 cm" -> "You used only the cm parts. Change both to cm first." Gap "635 cm" -> "635 is the two lengths added. The difference is the longer minus the shorter." The gap bracket pulses.
- Statue pair not right -> "These two are 20 m apart. Look for two statues whose tops are almost level." (least) or "These two are 54 m apart. Look for one tall and one short statue." (largest); the gap shown is the chosen pair's own and the two statues pulse.
- Doubled statue misses the top -> "Doubled, the Statue of Liberty is 93 × 2 = 186 m, taller than the Statue of Unity. Look for a statue that reaches exactly the top." (Guanyin doubled is 216 m, Spring Temple Buddha 256 m, Christ the Redeemer 76 m.)
- Wrong rod after doubling -> "The doubled rod ends at 170 cm. Look for a rod that ends at the same place."
- Hints (3 levels): (1) "Are the two lengths in the same unit? What must you do before you compare them?" (2) the Change to cm buttons glow and the 100 cm ticks light up; (3) "Change the m by multiplying by 100 and add the cm that are left. Then compare the two numbers." and the cards show ready cm numbers.
- Edge cases: equal lengths end together ("no gap"); a 1 cm gap shows in the magnifying circle; 2 m 150 cm is allowed.
7. Ending
- Star Challenge 1 is done when the signs are <, >, <, =, =; Star Challenge 2 when all four parts are right.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "Change both lengths to the same unit before you compare." "The difference is the longer length minus the shorter length." "Doubling means × 2, so halve to find the length that doubles." Think and talk: "Is the bigger number always the longer length? When is it not?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Photos: pegboard workshop wall; sunny hill and sky; six statue cut-outs at true relative height. Flat drawing: Ritika holding a rod. Code-drawn: tape, rods, flaps, cards, sign box, gap bracket, magnifying circle, dashed copies. Language: simple English, each number with its unit.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Sonu's stole is 285 cm long and Shikha's stole is 2 m 60 cm long. Which is longer, and by how much?
2. First change both to cm. 2 m 60 cm = 2 × 100 + 60 = 260 cm.
3. The difference is the longer length minus the shorter length: 285 − 260 = 25 cm.
4. So Sonu's stole is longer by 25 cm.
5. Doubling a length means multiplying it by 2. A rope of 90 cm doubled is 90 × 2 = 180 cm.
6. To find the length that becomes 180 cm when doubled, halve it: 180 ÷ 2 = 90 cm.
7. Rule: the difference is the bigger length minus the smaller length in the same unit. To undo doubling, halve.

content.question: Sonu's stole is 285 cm long and Shikha's stole is 2 m 60 cm long (practice values). Which is longer and by how much? A third piece doubled is 180 cm long. How long is the third piece?
content.publication_text:
Worked example: Sonu's stole is 285 cm long and Shikha's stole is 2 m 60 cm long (practice values). Which is longer and by how much? A third piece doubled is 180 cm long. How long is the third piece?
1. Change 2 m 60 cm to cm: 2 × 100 + 60 = 260 cm.
2. Compare 285 and 260: 285 is more, so Sonu's stole is longer.
3. Subtract the smaller from the bigger: 285 − 260 = 25 cm.
4. A piece that doubled is 180 cm: doubling is × 2, so the piece is 180 ÷ 2 = 90 cm.
5. Check: 260 + 25 = 285 and 90 × 2 = 180.
Answer: Sonu's stole is longer by 25 cm, and the third piece is 90 cm long

content.text:
Change both lengths to the same unit, the smaller one, then compare the numbers.
The difference is the bigger length minus the smaller length in the same unit.
Doubling is × 2 and halving undoes it.

3. $(b)$: $55\text{ cm} + 200\text{ cm} = 255\text{ cm}$ and $200\text{ cm} + 54\text{ cm} = 254\text{ cm}$. $255$ is more than $254$, so the left side is more.

content.text:
1. List the heights from the tallest to the shortest: $182\text{ m}$, $128\text{ m}$, $108\text{ m}$, $93\text{ m}$, $91\text{ m}$, $38\text{ m}$.
2. Find the difference of each statue and the next one in the list: $182 - 128 = 54\text{ m}$, $128 - 108 = 20\text{ m}$, $108 - 93 = 15\text{ m}$, $93 - 91 = 2\text{ m}$, $91 - 38 = 53\text{ m}$.
3. Two statues that are not next to each other have a statue between them, so they differ by even more.
[Image: Let Us Compare: Ans3: solution]
4. The least difference is $2\text{ m}$, between the Statue of Liberty $(93\text{ m})$ and The Motherland Calls $(91\text{ m})$.
5. Check: $93 - 91 = 2$, and every other pair is farther apart.
Answer: The Statue of Liberty and The Motherland Calls, $2\text{ m}$ apart
[Image: Let Us Compare: Ans3: solution (continued)]

content.text:
1. If a statue doubled is $182\text{ m}$, its height is half of $182\text{ m}$.
2. $182 \div 2 = 91\text{ m}$.
3. The Motherland Calls is $91\text{ m}$ tall.
4. Check: $91 \times 2 = 182$, and no other statue has a height that doubles to $182$.
Answer: The Motherland Calls, $91\text{ m}$

media.title: Kilometre Track

tool_config.idea: See 1 km as 1,000 m and find how many equal ropes or stops fit along a distance and where they stand: the number of pieces is the distance divided by the length of one piece.
tool_config.title: Kilometre Track
tool_config.screen: The road outside the weaving centre, drawn as a long straight strip in a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation, with a kilometre scale along it marked every 100 m. The track strip is the largest object on screen, 1 km long in the rope stage and 3 km long in the race stage. A rope tray holds rope pieces of a chosen length (1,000 m, 100 m, 10 m, 200 m, 500 m, 250 m and the practice lengths), and a rope snaps end to end onto the track where the last one stopped. A stop tray holds stop markers: a water cup, a child, a red flag and a blue flag, and an interval box takes a length in m; Place stops puts a marker at every interval from the start, and a list beside the track shows the positions from the start in m and in km. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type with progress dots under it. Controls: pick a rope length and drag ropes onto the track; pick an interval and a marker and tap Place stops; Undo; type an answer into a box; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the track being worked), Reset (restores both tracks), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: ropes placed, the metres filled out of 1,000 m, the number of stops, and the list of positions.
feedback: Each rope snaps onto the track where the last rope stopped and the counter shows the metres filled, for example 4 ropes of 250 m fill 1,000 m, which is 1 km.
If the ropes run past the end of the track, the tool says: The track is only 1,000 m long. Take a rope away.
Place stops puts a marker at every interval from the start and lists the positions, and the tool says, for example: 3,000 ÷ 500 = 6, so there are 6 stops.
If the student places a stop at the start line, the tool says: Here the first stop is after the first interval, not at the start line. Try again.
A wrong count slides back with a clue such as: How many pieces of that length fit in the whole distance?
tool_config.done_when: All five practice cards are solved, the five ropes of the rope table are counted and the three questions of the Kilometre Race are answered.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): fill the 1 km track with ropes of 125 m. How many ropes? Answer: 8 ropes, because 1,000 ÷ 125 = 8.
Card 2 (practice values): fill the 1 km track with ropes of 50 m. How many ropes? Answer: 20 ropes, because 1,000 ÷ 50 = 20.

Card 3 (practice values): on a 2 km track place a marker after every 250 m and read the positions. Answer: 2,000 ÷ 250 = 8 markers, at 250 m, 500 m, 750 m, 1 km, 1 km 250 m, 1 km 500 m, 1 km 750 m and 2 km.

Card 4 (practice values): on the same 2 km track compare an interval of 400 m with an interval of 200 m. Answer: 5 stops for 400 m and 10 stops for 200 m, because 2,000 ÷ 400 = 5 and 2,000 ÷ 200 = 10. A smaller interval gives more stops.
Card 5: drag a marker to 1 km 500 m on the track and type its position in m. Answer: 1,500 m, because 1 × 1,000 + 500 = 1,500.
Challenge: 'Ropes of different lengths are used to make 1 km.' How many ropes of 100 m, 10 m, 200 m, 500 m and 250 m make 1 km? Answer: 10, 100, 5, 2 and 4 ropes.

Challenge: 'Sheena and Jennifer are helping to organise a 3 km race.' Water stations after every 500 m: how many, and where? Children at an interval of 300 m: how many, and where? Red and blue flags alternately at every 50 m: how many? Answer: 6 water stations at 500 m, 1 km, 1 km 500 m, 2 km, 2 km 500 m and 3 km; 10 children at every 300 m from 300 m to 3,000 m; 60 flags, 30 red and 30 blue.

hint_ladder.text: How many metres are in the whole distance? Change km to m first.
How long is one piece? How many pieces of that length fill the whole distance?
Divide the whole distance in m by the length of one piece. The stops stand at 1, 2, 3 and so on times the length of one piece.
The tool fills the track piece by piece and counts them for you: the number of pieces is the answer.

media.instructions_for_student: The student will understand that 1 km is 1,000 m, and that the number of equal pieces along a distance is the distance in m divided by the length of one piece.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Kilometre Track
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M2.S7.T7.C27.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Far and Near, "Measuring Long Distances": the walk and count steps activity, the rope table for 1 km and the "Kilometre Race" (3 km; every 500 m, 300 m, 50 m). Practice values added: 40 m ropes, a 4 km road with stops every 800 m, 2 km 300 m, 125 steps for 100 m, places at 120 m, 400 m, 1,600 m (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that 1 km is 1,000 m, and finds how many equal ropes or stops fit along a distance and where each stop stands, by dividing the distance in m by the length of one piece.
- Out of scope: mm and cm, adding or subtracting distances, travel time.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A bird's-eye photo of a straight village road with green fields: a strip across the stage with a tick every 100 m, a bold labelled tick every 1 km, and signposts "0" and "1 km". A counter above reads "Ropes: 0   Metres filled: 0 of 1,000". Below lies a tray of coiled ropes with a "40 m" rope; flat-drawn Sheena and Jennifer stand at the start.
- Instruction line: "Fill the 1 km road with ropes of 40 m." The child is invited to drag the rope to the start.
2. Scene and Objects
- Road strip: 90% of the stage width; 1 km (Activity 1, rope table), 4 km (Activities 2 and 3) or 3 km (race), always fitting.
- Ropes: labelled coils. A rope dropped on the road lies from the start; a copy handle at its right end is pulled along the road to lay whole ropes end to end, and the counter updates.
- Stop markers: a water cup (photo), a child with a raised hand (flat drawing), a red flag, a blue flag. A marker dropped on the road snaps to the nearest 100 m (50 m for flags) with a bubble showing its distance from the start. A repeat handle on the first marker lays markers at the same gap as far as it is pulled.
- Positions strip under the road lists the stops, for example "800 m, 1 km 600 m"; three count chips above the road. Goal chip, for example "1,000 m with ropes of 40 m". Pills: 1, 2, 3, star, star, star.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag a rope to the start and pull its handle; pulling back takes ropes away; a rope past the end turns red. Drag a marker to the first stop and pull the repeat handle; drag a marker off the road to remove it. Tap a count chip to commit a number.
- Bottom buttons: Hint, Check (becomes Next when done), Reset. Undo is a small back arrow; retry is free.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Fill the 1 km road with ropes of 40 m." Chip: "1,000 m with ropes of 40 m". Setup: a dashed outline of one rope. Guess: the child taps the number of ropes: "10", "25" or "250". The child drags the rope to the start and pulls the handle to the end. Result: the counter stops at 25 and the road turns green: "25 ropes of 40 m fill 1,000 m, because 1,000 ÷ 40 = 25." Help: guided.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "A 4 km road has a water cup after every 800 m. Place the cups." Chip: "4 km, a cup every 800 m". Setup: a 4 km road, one cup. Guess: the child taps the number of cups: "4", "5" or "6". The child drops the cup at 800 m and pulls the repeat handle to the finish line. Result: the strip lists 800 m, 1 km 600 m, 2 km 400 m, 3 km 200 m, 4 km: "4 km is 4,000 m, and 4,000 ÷ 800 = 5 cups. The last cup is at the finish line." Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Drag the flag to 2 km 300 m. How many m is that?" Chip: "2 km 300 m is ___ m". Setup: the 4 km road, a red flag. Guess: the child drops the flag where they think 2 km 300 m is, then taps "2,300 m", "500 m" or "230 m". Result: the flag sits on the 23rd tick: "2 km is 2 × 1,000 = 2,000 m, and 2,000 m + 300 m is 2,300 m." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1 (the book's question). Goal line: "Ropes of different lengths are used to make 1 km. Find how many ropes of each length are needed to make 1 km." Chip: "5 rope lengths". Setup: a table at the top of the stage: "1,000 m: 1 rope" (given) and empty rows "100 m", "10 m", "200 m", "500 m", "250 m". The child taps a row, taps a count chip (guess), pulls ropes to the end of the road and presses Check; the counter fills the row. Answers: 10, 100, 5, 2, 4; result, for example "1,000 ÷ 250 = 4 ropes." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2 (the book's question). Goal line: "Sheena and Jennifer are helping to organise a 3 km race. Help them with the arrangements for the race." Chip: "3 km race". Three tabs on a 3 km road: tap a count chip, drop the first marker, pull the handle to the finish line, Check. (a) "Water stations are to be arranged after every 500 m. How many water stations must be set up? At what positions from the starting point will these water stations be placed?" Chips "5", "6", "7". Result: "3 km is 3,000 m and 3,000 ÷ 500 = 6 stations", at 500 m, 1 km, 1 km 500 m, 2 km, 2 km 500 m and 3 km. (b) "Children need to stand at an interval of 300 m to direct the runners. How many children are needed? At what positions from the starting point will the children be standing?" Chips "9", "10", "11". Result: "3,000 ÷ 300 = 10 children", at every 300 m from 300 m to 3,000 m. (c) "Red and blue flags are to be placed alternately at every 50 m. How many red and blue flags are needed till the finish line?" The flags lay red, blue, red, blue; two chip rows, red and blue, each "29", "30", "31". Result: "3,000 ÷ 50 = 60 flags, 30 red and 30 blue." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3 (the book's question). Goal line: "Walk on the lines and count the number of steps." Chip: "Steps and distances". Setup: a playground from above with painted lines "100 m" and "200 m", a flag at each end, a flat-drawn child, a round "Walk" button. Part 1: the child holds Walk and a counter ticks to the flag: practice values, 125 steps for 100 m, 250 steps for 200 m. Guess before the 200 m line: "more than 125 steps", "125 steps" or "250 steps". Part 2: a strip with Home and pins "Tea shop 120 m", "School gate 400 m", "Temple 1,600 m"; for each pin the child taps its steps from three chips (right: 150, 500, 2,000; wrong: the metres as steps, and a number too small). Part 3, the book's parts: "Identify and write the locations that are the nearest and the farthest from your home." (drag two pins to the slots "Nearest location" and "Farthest location"); "Write the distances obtained above in increasing order." (drag three tags into three slots); "Name a location that is equal to or more than 1,000 m from your home." (tap a pin). Result: the tea shop, the temple; 120 m, 400 m, 1,600 m; the temple is 1 km 600 m. The strip ends "These are practice values. Your own school and home will give different numbers." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Pulling the handle shows that a shorter rope needs more ropes (25 of 40 m, 100 of 10 m) and that the count is 1,000 ÷ the length of one piece. The repeat handle shows that stops stand at 1, 2, 3 and so on times the first gap.
- Rules in the child's words: 1 km is 1,000 m; change the distance to m first; the number of pieces is the distance divided by one piece; the last stop is at the finish line.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the road or marker and the goal chip turn green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick and Next unlocks. Confetti only at the end.
- Wrong (every case): red strip, a small shake, ONE friendly line; no score; try again.
- Ropes pulled past the end -> "The road is only 1,000 m long. Take a rope away." Road not full -> "There is still road left. Pull one more rope."
- Marker at 0 m -> "The first stop is after the first gap, not at the start line." Wrong first gap -> "The question says every 500 m, but the first marker is at 300 m."
- Count off by one (for example "7" cups) -> "Count the markers on the track. The first stop is after 500 m and the last is at the finish line." For "5": "The last stop is at the finish line, so count it too." A marker dragged past the finish line slides back.
- 2 km 300 m as "500 m" -> "1 km is 1,000 m, not 100 m. Look at the 1 km tick." As "230 m" -> "2 km is 2,000 m. Put the 300 m after it."
- Walk steps equal to metres (for example "120 steps") -> "100 m took 125 steps, so 120 m takes more than 120 steps. Look at the 100 m line."
- Hints (3 levels): (1) "How many metres are in the whole distance? Change km to m first." (2) the whole road in m is written on the signpost and one piece is outlined; (3) "Divide the whole distance in m by the length of one piece. The stops stand at 1, 2, 3 and so on times the length of one piece." and the first piece or stop is placed.
7. Ending
- Done: Star 1 when the rows read 10, 100, 5, 2 and 4; Star 2 when 6 stations, 10 children and 60 flags (30 red, 30 blue) are right; Star 3 when the pins, the order and the 1,000 m place are right.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "1 km is 1,000 m." "The number of pieces is the whole distance divided by the length of one piece." "The stops stand at 1, 2, 3 and so on times the gap." Think and talk: "If the gap between flags gets smaller, do you need more flags or fewer? Why?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Photos: village road from above; school playground from above; coiled ropes; water cup; red and blue flags. Flat drawings: Sheena, Jennifer, a child with a raised hand, a walking child. Code-drawn: road strip, signposts, handles, counters, strips, table. Language: simple English.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a 2 km cycle track has a flag after every 400 m. How many flags are needed, and where do they stand?
2. First change 2 km to m: 2 km = 2 × 1,000 = 2,000 m.
3. Each piece of the track is 400 m long, so divide: 2,000 ÷ 400 = 5 pieces, and so 5 flags.
4. The flags stand at 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 times 400 m from the start: 400 m, 800 m, 1,200 m, 1,600 m and 2,000 m. The last flag is at the end.
5. The same idea tells how many ropes make 1 km. If every rope is 125 m long, 1,000 ÷ 125 = 8 ropes make 1 km.
6. Rule: the number of equal pieces is the whole distance ÷ the length of one piece. The stops stand at 1, 2, 3 and so on times the length of one piece.

media.teaching_notes: 1. This is an activity at your school and near your home. The numbers below are practice values that show how to do it. Yours will differ. 2. Use a long tape to measure 100 m and 200 m on the playground, mark the points and walk each line, counting steps. Practice values: 100 m takes 125 steps and 200 m takes 250 steps. 3. Find the length of one step: 100 m = 100 × 100 = 10,000 cm, and 10,000 ÷ 125 = 80 cm. So one step is 80 cm. 4. Use the step to find other distances. A tea shop is 120 m away: 12,000 ÷ 80 = 150 steps. A school gate is 400 m away: 40,000 ÷ 80 = 500 steps. A temple is 1,600 m away: 160,000 ÷ 80 = 2,000 steps. 5. (a): The nearest is the tea shop, 120 m. The farthest is the temple, 1,600 m. 6. (b): In increasing order: 120 m, 400 m, 1,600 m. 7. (c): The temple is more than 1,000 m away: 1,600 m = 1 km 600 m. 8. Check: 125 × 80 = 10,000 cm, which is 100 m. Answer: Sample answer, practice values: nearest 120 m; farthest 1,600 m; in order 120 m, 400 m, 1,600 m; (c): 1 km 600 m. Your answer may differ.

content.text: Measure $100\text{ m}$ and $200\text{ m}$ on your school playground, or any other place in and around your school, using a long tape. Mark these points and draw a straight line. Walk on the lines and count the number of steps. Use this relationship between the number of steps taken and distance walked to find distances around you for at least $3$ locations. Wherever possible, walk and find the number of steps. Otherwise, find the distance and estimate the number of steps. $(a)$: Identify and write the locations that are the nearest and the farthest from your home. $(b)$: Write the distances obtained above in increasing order. $(c)$: Name a location that is equal to or more than $1,000\text{ m}$ from your home.

content.text:
1. This is an activity at your school and near your home. The numbers below are practice values that show how to do it. Yours will differ.
2. Use a long tape to measure $100\text{ m}$ and $200\text{ m}$ on the playground, mark the points and walk each line, counting steps. Practice values: $100\text{ m}$ takes $125$ steps and $200\text{ m}$ takes $250$ steps.
3. Find the length of one step: $100\text{ m} = 100 \times 100 = 10,000\text{ cm}$, and $10,000 \div 125 = 80\text{ cm}$. So one step is $80\text{ cm}$.
[Image: Measuring Long Distances: Ans1: solution]
4. Use the step to find other distances. A tea shop is $120\text{ m}$ away: $12,000 \div 80 = 150$ steps. A school gate is $400\text{ m}$ away: $40,000 \div 80 = 500$ steps. A temple is $1,600\text{ m}$ away: $160,000 \div 80 = 2,000$ steps.
5. $(a)$: The nearest is the tea shop, $120\text{ m}$. The farthest is the temple, $1,600\text{ m}$.
6. $(b)$: In increasing order: $120\text{ m}$, $400\text{ m}$, $1,600\text{ m}$.
7. $(c)$: The temple is more than $1,000\text{ m}$ away: $1,600\text{ m} = 1\text{ km } 600\text{ m}$.
8. Check: $125 \times 80 = 10,000\text{ cm}$, which is $100\text{ m}$.
Answer: Sample answer, practice values: nearest $120\text{ m}$; farthest $1,600\text{ m}$; in order $120\text{ m}$, $400\text{ m}$, $1,600\text{ m}$; $(c)$: $1\text{ km } 600\text{ m}$. Your answer may differ.
[Image: Measuring Long Distances: Ans1: solution (continued)]

content.text: Ropes of different lengths are used to make $1\text{ km}$. Find how many ropes of each length are needed to make $1\text{ km}$. A rope of $1,000\text{ m}$: $1$ rope. $(a)$: a rope of $100\text{ m}$: $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$ ropes; $(b)$: a rope of $10\text{ m}$: $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$ ropes; $(c)$: a rope of $200\text{ m}$: $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$ ropes; $(d)$: a rope of $500\text{ m}$: $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$ ropes; $(e)$: a rope of $250\text{ m}$: $\underline{\hspace{1.2em}}$ ropes.

content.text:
1. $1\text{ km} = 1,000\text{ m}$. The number of ropes $= 1,000 \div$ the length of one rope.
2. $(a)$: $100\text{ m}$: $1,000 \div 100 = 10$ ropes.
3. $(b)$: $10\text{ m}$: $1,000 \div 10 = 100$ ropes.
4. $(c)$: $200\text{ m}$: $1,000 \div 200 = 5$ ropes.
5. $(d)$: $500\text{ m}$: $1,000 \div 500 = 2$ ropes.
6. $(e)$: $250\text{ m}$: $1,000 \div 250 = 4$ ropes.
[Image: Measuring Long Distances: Ans2: solution]
7. Check: a shorter rope needs more ropes. $10\text{ m}$ is the shortest rope and needs the most, $100$ ropes.
Answer: $(a)$: $10$; $(b)$: $100$; $(c)$: $5$; $(d)$: $2$; $(e)$: $4$
[Image: Measuring Long Distances: Ans2: solution (continued)]

content.text:
1. Change $3\text{ km}$ to m: $3 \times 1,000 = 3,000\text{ m}$.
2. A water station after every $500\text{ m}$: $3,000 \div 500 = 6$ stations. The last one is at the finish line.
3. The stations stand at $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $5$ and $6$ times $500\text{ m}$ from the start.
4. Positions: $500\text{ m}$, $1\text{ km}$, $1\text{ km } 500\text{ m}$, $2\text{ km}$, $2\text{ km } 500\text{ m}$ and $3\text{ km}$.
5. Check: $6 \times 500 = 3,000\text{ m}$, the whole race.
Answer: $6$ stations, at $500\text{ m}$, $1\text{ km}$, $1\text{ km } 500\text{ m}$, $2\text{ km}$, $2\text{ km } 500\text{ m}$ and $3\text{ km}$

The stations stand at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 times 500 m from the start.
Positions: 500 m, 1 km, 1 km 500 m, 2 km, 2 km 500 m and 3 km.
Check: 6 × 500 = 3,000 m, the whole race.

content.book_number: Kilometre Race: Q3 flags
content.question_tex: Sheena and Jennifer are helping to organise a $3\text{ km}$ race. Red and blue flags are to be placed alternately at every $50\text{ m}$. How many red and blue flags are needed till the finish line?
content.publication_text: Sheena and Jennifer are helping to organise a $3\text{ km}$ race. Red and blue flags are to be placed alternately at every $50\text{ m}$. How many red and blue flags are needed till the finish line?

content.text:
1. Change $3\text{ km}$ to m: $3 \times 1,000 = 3,000\text{ m}$.
2. A flag at every $50\text{ m}$: $3,000 \div 50 = 60$ flags till the finish line. The first flag is at $50\text{ m}$ and the last is at the finish line.
3. The flags are red and blue by turns: red, blue, red, blue and so on. Half are red and half are blue.
4. $60 \div 2 = 30$, so there are $30$ red flags and $30$ blue flags.
5. Check: $30 + 30 = 60$, and $60 \times 50 = 3,000\text{ m}$.
Answer: $60$ flags: $30$ red and $30$ blue

media.title: Millimetre Ruler

tool_config.idea: Read and draw lengths in cm and mm using the small marks of a ruler: a length is the cm mark before its end plus the number of small marks after it, and 1 cm = 10 mm.
tool_config.title: Millimetre Ruler
tool_config.screen: The ruler desk of the village weaving centre, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A big yellow ruler, the largest object on screen, is marked in cm with 10 equal parts in every cm: the cm marks are long and numbered, the 5 mm marks are medium and the other marks are short, so there are 9 small marks between two cm marks. A zoom lens on a handle magnifies the centimetre it covers. A line lies on the ruler with a draggable end point that snaps to each mm mark, and objects to measure (a sprout, a small screw and a nail, with practice lengths) lie beside the ruler. A read-out shows the length in two forms, for example 4 cm 6 mm = 46 mm. The design of four nested shapes in your maths book can be placed on the desk with its eight lines, each line with a box for cm and mm. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type with progress dots under it. Controls: drag the end of the line along the ruler; tap the lens to zoom; type into the cm box and the mm box; drag the ruler along a line of the design; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the line of this card), Reset (restores the ruler and the objects), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the length in cm and mm, the length in mm, and a card number out of 7.
feedback: The end point snaps to the nearest mm mark and the read-out says the length, for example: 4 cm and 6 small marks, 4 cm 6 mm, which is 46 mm.
If the student reads only the cm mark, the tool says: The line goes past the 4 cm mark. Count the small marks after it.
The lens makes the small marks big so that they can be counted one by one, and the counted marks light up in turn.
A wrong mm number slides back with a clue such as: Each small mark is 1 mm. Count again from the cm mark.
In the design, the ruler lays itself along the chosen line and the tool says the length only after the student has typed a reading.
tool_config.done_when: All five practice cards are solved, the small marks are counted, the eight lines of the design are measured and the five lines are drawn.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): the sprout ends on the 4th small mark after the 2 cm mark. Read its length. Answer: 2 cm 4 mm = 2 × 10 + 4 = 24 mm.
Card 2 (practice values): the screw ends on the 9th small mark after the 3 cm mark. Read its length. Answer: 3 cm 9 mm = 3 × 10 + 9 = 39 mm.
Card 3 (practice values): drag the end of a line to draw 4 cm 6 mm, then write it in mm. Answer: 4 × 10 + 6 = 46 mm.
Card 4 (practice values): drag the end of a line to draw 72 mm and write it in cm and mm. Answer: 72 mm = 70 mm + 2 mm = 7 cm 2 mm.
Card 5 (practice values): a nail is 2 cm 8 mm long and a bead is 25 mm long. Which is longer, and by how much? Answer: 2 cm 8 mm = 28 mm and 28 − 25 = 3 mm, so the nail is longer by 3 mm.

Challenge: 'Let us look at the scale. Do you notice the small marks between 1 cm and 2 cm? Count how many marks there are between 1 cm and 2 cm.' Then: 'Measure the lines in the design and write their measurements in cm and mm.' Answer: 9 small marks; the eight lines measure 48 mm, 35 mm, 60 mm, 27 mm, 22 mm, 19 mm, 44 mm and 61 mm, which are 4 cm 8 mm, 3 cm 5 mm, 6 cm, 2 cm 7 mm, 2 cm 2 mm, 1 cm 9 mm, 4 cm 4 mm and 6 cm 1 mm. A ruler may read 1 mm different.

Challenge: 'Draw lines of the following lengths in your notebook using a scale.' 5 cm 5 mm, 3 cm 6 mm, 8 cm 3 mm, 36 mm and 67 mm. Answer: 55 mm, 36 mm, 83 mm, 3 cm 6 mm and 6 cm 7 mm. The sprout diary needs real seeds and is done at home.

hint_ladder.text: Which centimetre mark is just before the end of the line?
Count the small marks after that centimetre mark. Each small mark is 1 mm.
Write the cm and the mm. In mm only, the cm are multiplied by 10 and the mm are added.
The tool puts the end point on the right mark and shows the length in cm and mm and in mm.

student_does: Look at the video's ruler with the lens on 1 cm, cut into 10 equal parts. Count the small marks between two cm marks, then press Next.
Read the length of a sprout and a screw on the ruler in cm and mm, drag the end of a line to draw a given length, and write each length in mm only.
Do your maths book's own tasks: count the small marks between 1 cm and 2 cm, measure the eight lines of the design in cm and mm, and draw lines of 5 cm 5 mm, 3 cm 6 mm, 8 cm 3 mm, 36 mm and 67 mm.
tool_questions: Card 1 (practice values): the sprout ends on the 4th small mark after the 2 cm mark. Read its length. Answer: 2 cm 4 mm = 2 × 10 + 4 = 24 mm.
Card 2 (practice values): the screw ends on the 9th small mark after the 3 cm mark. Read its length. Answer: 3 cm 9 mm = 3 × 10 + 9 = 39 mm.
Card 3 (practice values): drag the end of a line to draw 4 cm 6 mm, then write it in mm. Answer: 4 × 10 + 6 = 46 mm.
Card 4 (practice values): drag the end of a line to draw 72 mm and write it in cm and mm. Answer: 72 mm = 70 mm + 2 mm = 7 cm 2 mm.
Card 5 (practice values): a nail is 2 cm 8 mm long and a bead is 25 mm long. Which is longer, and by how much? Answer: 2 cm 8 mm = 28 mm and 28 − 25 = 3 mm, so the nail is longer by 3 mm.

Challenge: 'Let us look at the scale. Do you notice the small marks between 1 cm and 2 cm? Count how many marks there are between 1 cm and 2 cm.' Then: 'Measure the lines in the design and write their measurements in cm and mm.' Answer: 9 small marks; the eight lines measure 48 mm, 35 mm, 60 mm, 27 mm, 22 mm, 19 mm, 44 mm and 61 mm, which are 4 cm 8 mm, 3 cm 5 mm, 6 cm, 2 cm 7 mm, 2 cm 2 mm, 1 cm 9 mm, 4 cm 4 mm and 6 cm 1 mm. A ruler may read 1 mm different.

Challenge: 'Draw lines of the following lengths in your notebook using a scale.' 5 cm 5 mm, 3 cm 6 mm, 8 cm 3 mm, 36 mm and 67 mm. Answer: 55 mm, 36 mm, 83 mm, 3 cm 6 mm and 6 cm 7 mm. The sprout diary needs real seeds and is done at home.

media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Millimetre Ruler
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M2.S12.T12.C52.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Far and Near, "The World of Small Things": count the small marks between 1 cm and 2 cm, "Let Us Measure" (the design with eight lines), the sprout diary, and "Let Us Draw" (5 cm 5 mm, 3 cm 6 mm, 8 cm 3 mm, 36 mm, 67 mm). Practice values added: 2 cm 4 mm, 3 cm 9 mm, 5 cm 8 mm, 94 mm (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student reads and draws small lengths with the small marks of a ruler, and sees that 1 cm is 10 mm, so a length in cm and mm can be written in mm.
- Out of scope: changing m or km to mm, adding or comparing lengths.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A wooden ruler desk (photo). A big yellow ruler (code-drawn, 0 to 12 cm) lies across the stage: long numbered marks at each cm, a medium mark at each 5 mm, short marks at each mm. A round magnifying lens sits on the 1 cm to 2 cm part and shows its ten equal parts. A sprout (photo cut-out) lies along the ruler from the 0 mark, its tip a little past the 2 cm mark.
- Instruction line: "Read the sprout: the cm first, then the small marks."
- The child is invited to turn the two reading wheels under the ruler.
2. Scene and Objects
- Ruler: about 90% of the stage width; each mm is wide enough to tap. Lens: drag it along the ruler; it magnifies one cm and numbers the small marks 1 to 9 when tapped.
- Objects on the ruler, each starting at 0: a sprout, a small screw, a nail (photo cut-outs). Thread: a thin thread (a sprout is bendy) that lies along a sprout and straightens onto the ruler.
- Reading wheels under the ruler: a "cm" wheel (0 to 12) and a "mm" wheel (0 to 9). They move a thin needle on the ruler live, so the child sees where the reading lands. A third "in mm" box of up to three digits appears when asked.
- Drawing: a notebook page (photo) under the ruler with a start dot; the line end is a round handle that snaps to each mm mark.
- Design (Star Challenge 1): four nested four-sided shapes, a big outer shape, a large diamond, a rectangle and a small tilted shape, drawn at the ruler's scale, with the eight lines numbered 1 to 8 from top to bottom.
- Goal chip at the top left, for example "Sprout: ? cm ? mm". Pills: 1, 2, 3, 4, star, star, star.
3. Main Interaction
- Turn a wheel by tapping its arrows or dragging; Check compares the reading with the true length. Tap a line of the design: the ruler turns and lies along it with 0 at its start. Tap a sprout: its thread straightens onto the ruler. Drag a line end to draw.
- Bottom buttons: Hint, Check (becomes Next when done), Reset. Undo is a small back arrow; retry is free.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Read the sprout: the cm first, then the small marks." Chip: "Sprout: ? cm ? mm". Setup: a sprout ending on the 4th small mark after 2 cm; the lens on 2 cm; the marks numbered. Guess: the child turns the cm wheel to the cm mark the sprout has passed. Then the mm wheel to the number of small marks, and the "in mm" box. Result: the needle meets the tip: "2 cm 4 mm is 2 × 10 + 4 = 24 mm." Help: guided, lens and numbers.
- Activity 2 (independent). Goal line: "Read the screw: the cm first, then the small marks." Chip: "Screw: ? cm ? mm". Setup: a screw ending on the 9th small mark after 3 cm; no lens, no numbers. Guess: the child taps "less than 4 cm" or "more than 4 cm" first. Result: "3 cm 9 mm is 3 × 10 + 9 = 39 mm. It is just less than 4 cm." Help: independent.
- Activity 3 (guided). Goal line: "Draw a line of 5 cm 8 mm." Chip: "Line: 5 cm 8 mm". Setup: the notebook page, the line end at 0, a live read-out "0 cm 0 mm". Guess: the child taps "58 mm", "508 mm" or "13 mm" for its length in mm. The child drags the end to 5 cm 8 mm. Result: "5 cm 8 mm is 5 × 10 + 8 = 58 mm." Help: guided, live read-out and lens.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Draw a line of 94 mm. How many cm and mm is that?" Chip: "94 mm is ? cm ? mm". Setup: the line end at 0, no read-out. Guess: before drawing, the child taps "9 cm 4 mm", "4 cm 9 mm" or "94 cm". The child drags the end, then sets the wheels. Result: "94 is 90 + 4, so 94 mm is 9 cm 4 mm." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1 (the book's question, two parts). Goal line: "Let us look at the scale. Do you notice the small marks between 1 cm and 2 cm? Count how many marks there are between 1 cm and 2 cm." Chip: "Count the marks". The lens is on 1 cm to 2 cm; the child taps a count chip first ("8", "9", "10"), taps the small marks one by one, then Check. Result: "There are 9 small marks. They cut 1 cm into 10 parts of 1 mm." Part 2, goal line: "Measure the lines in the design and write their measurements in cm and mm." Chip: "8 lines". The child taps line (1) to (8); the ruler lies along it; the child turns the cm and mm wheels, Check. Answers: 4 cm 8 mm, 3 cm 5 mm, 6 cm, 2 cm 7 mm, 2 cm 2 mm, 1 cm 9 mm, 4 cm 4 mm and 6 cm 1 mm (48, 35, 60, 27, 22, 19, 44 and 61 mm). A reading within 1 mm is accepted with "Your ruler may read 1 mm different: that is fine." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2 (the book's question). Goal line: "Over the next 4 days, take out one seed each day and measure the length of sprout." Chip: "Sprout diary". Setup: four sprout photos, Day 1 to Day 4, each with a thread, and a table Day 1 to Day 4 at the top of the stage with an empty box per day. Practice values: 3 mm, 9 mm, 16 mm and 25 mm. Guess: for Day 1, "less than 1 cm" or "more than 1 cm". The child taps a sprout, the thread straightens onto the ruler, the child sets the "in mm" box and Check fills the table. Result: "Each day the sprout is longer: 3, 9, 16, 25 mm. Your own sprouts will give different numbers." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3 (the book's question). Goal line: "Draw lines of the following lengths in your notebook using a scale." Chip: "5 lines". Five tabs: (a) "5 cm 5 mm", (b) "3 cm 6 mm", (c) "8 cm 3 mm", (d) "36 mm", (e) "67 mm". The child drags the end to the length; the read-out is hidden; Check. Answers in mm: 55, 36, 83, 36, 67. Result for (d): the line lies exactly on the line of (b): "36 mm is 30 mm + 6 mm, which is 3 cm 6 mm, the same as (b)." Guess: before (b) to (e), "longer than the last line" or "shorter than the last line". Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Counting the 9 small marks and seeing the lens split 1 cm into 10 equal parts shows that 1 cm is 10 mm. A length is the cm mark just before the end plus the small marks after it. The tens of mm are cm and the ones are mm.
- Rules in the child's words: 1 cm is 10 mm; read the cm first, then count the small marks; 46 mm is 4 cm 6 mm.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the needle and the goal chip turn green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick and Next unlocks. Confetti only on the end screen.
- Wrong (every case): red strip, a small shake, ONE friendly line; no score; try again.
- mm left at 0 -> "The line goes past the 3 cm mark. Count the small marks after it." The marks after 3 cm pulse.
- Off by one -> "Start counting at the first small mark after the cm mark, not at the cm mark." The first small mark pulses.
- 4 cm 6 mm written as 406 mm -> "1 cm is 10 mm, not 100 mm. 4 cm is 40 mm." The 4 cm part pulses.
- The medium 5 mm mark read as 5 cm -> "The longer mark in the middle is 5 mm, not 5 cm."
- Drawn line wrong -> "Your line is 5 cm 6 mm long. The card asks for 5 cm 8 mm. Count the small marks after 5 cm." (own numbers each time). 94 mm as 4 cm 9 mm -> "94 mm is 9 tens and 4 ones: 9 cm and 4 mm."
- Hints (3 levels): (1) "Which centimetre mark is just before the end of the line?" (2) the lens zooms on that cm and the small marks light up one by one; (3) "Write the cm and the mm. In mm only, multiply the cm by 10 and add the mm." and the needle jumps to the right mark.
- Edge cases: a reading of exactly a cm mark has 0 mm (the design line of 60 mm is 6 cm); a line of under 1 cm (3 mm) has 0 cm; the lines (b) and (d) are equal.
7. Ending
- Star 1 is done when 9 and all eight lengths are right; Star 2 when the table has 3, 9, 16, 25 mm; Star 3 when the five lines are drawn.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "1 cm is 10 mm." "Read the cm first, then count the small marks." "Tens of mm make cm, so 46 mm is 4 cm 6 mm." Think and talk: "Why do we need mm as well as cm?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Photos: wooden desk, notebook page, sprout, small screw, nail, four sprouts with seeds. Code-drawn: ruler with marks, lens, thread, needle, wheels, design, table. Language: simple English; each length with its unit.

content.text:
One centimetre is divided into ten equal parts. Each part is called 1 millimetre (mm).
1 cm = 10 mm
These small marks between any two centimetre marks help us measure the smaller lengths. Thus, it adds to the precision in measurement.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a sprout, a small screw and a nail are shorter than most things you measure. How can you measure them? How many small marks are there between 1 cm and 2 cm on a ruler?
2. Look at a ruler. Between any two centimetre marks there are 9 small marks. They cut 1 cm into 10 equal parts.
3. Each part is called 1 millimetre, written 1 mm. So 1 cm = 10 mm.
4. The small marks help us measure smaller lengths and give a more exact measurement. A sprout, a small screw or a nail can be measured with them.
5. To change cm to mm, multiply by 10: 3 cm = 3 × 10 = 30 mm.
6. A length of 8 mm is less than 1 cm, because 8 is less than 10.
7. Rule: 1 cm = 10 mm, so multiply by 10 to change cm to mm.

3. To write it in mm, change the cm to mm and add the rest: 4 cm 6 mm = 4 × 10 + 6 = 46 mm.
4. To draw a length given in mm, split it into tens and ones. 72 mm is 70 mm + 2 mm = 7 cm 2 mm. Put the 0 of the scale at the start, go to the 7 cm mark, then 2 small marks more.
5. The same works for any length in mm. 52 mm is 5 cm 2 mm: go to the 5 cm mark and then 2 small marks more. The tens of mm are cm and the ones are the small marks.
6. Rule: the tens of mm are cm and the ones are mm, so 46 mm is 4 cm 6 mm.

7. Check: 7 × 10 + 2 = 72 mm.
Answer: 4 cm 6 mm = 46 mm, and a line of 72 mm is drawn to 7 cm 2 mm

content.text:
1. Put the $0$ of the scale at the start of the line and mark the end at the length asked.
2. $(a)$: $5\text{ cm } 5\text{ mm}$: go to $5\text{ cm}$ and then $5$ small marks. In mm that is $5 \times 10 + 5 = 55\text{ mm}$.
3. $(b)$: $3\text{ cm } 6\text{ mm}$: go to $3\text{ cm}$ and then $6$ small marks. In mm that is $3 \times 10 + 6 = 36\text{ mm}$.
4. $(c)$: $8\text{ cm } 3\text{ mm}$: go to $8\text{ cm}$ and then $3$ small marks. In mm that is $8 \times 10 + 3 = 83\text{ mm}$.
[Image: The World of Small Things: Ans4: solution]
5. $(d)$: $36\text{ mm} = 30\text{ mm} + 6\text{ mm} = 3\text{ cm } 6\text{ mm}$, the same length as $(b)$.
6. $(e)$: $67\text{ mm} = 60\text{ mm} + 7\text{ mm} = 6\text{ cm } 7\text{ mm}$: go to $6\text{ cm}$ and then $7$ small marks.
7. Check: the lines in $(b)$ and $(d)$ are equal, and $(c)$ is the longest of the five.
Answer: $(a)$: $55\text{ mm}$; $(b)$: $36\text{ mm}$; $(c)$: $83\text{ mm}$; $(d)$: $3\text{ cm } 6\text{ mm}$; $(e)$: $6\text{ cm } 7\text{ mm}$

media.title: Double Number Line

tool_config.idea: Change a length from one unit to another with the multipliers 10, 100 and 1,000 on two linked number lines, and split a length into a part in the bigger unit and a rest in the smaller unit.
tool_config.title: Double Number Line
tool_config.screen: A pair of tapes on the weaving centre wall, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation: the top tape in the bigger unit and the bottom tape in the smaller unit, with their ticks lined up one under the other. The two lines are the largest object on screen. A draggable pointer moves along both tapes together, so one tick shows the same length in two units. A unit switch picks cm over mm, m over cm or km over m. Multiplier boxes sit on the arrows between the tapes (for example ×10 from the top tape down to the bottom tape) and take a number. Tick labels may be blank for the student to fill in. Under the tapes a split tray cuts a length such as 5,792 cm into a part that is whole metres (5,700 cm) and a rest (92 cm), and joins them as 57 m 92 cm. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type with progress dots under it. Controls: drag the pointer; tap a blank label and type a number; tap a multiplier box and type; drag the split mark in the tray; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the blanks of this card), Reset (restores the lines), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the same length on both tapes, the multiplier used, the split parts, and a card number out of 7.
feedback: The pointer moves on both tapes at once and the read-out shows both numbers with their units and the multiplier, for example: 6 cm is 6 × 10 = 60 mm.
A blank label accepts only the number that belongs to that tick. A wrong number slides back with a clue such as: Going down the multiplier is 10, so multiply the top number by 10.
A multiplier box is checked against the two numbers above and below it, and the tool says, for example: ×10 is right because 7 × 10 = 70.
In the split tray the part in the bigger unit and the rest are shown in two colours, and the tool says: 5,700 cm is 57 m, and 92 cm are left, so 57 m 92 cm.
In the conversion tasks the tool says whether the answer is right and gives a clue; it never fills the answer in before the third hint.
tool_config.done_when: All five practice cards are solved, the three number lines are filled in, and the fourteen conversions are answered.
