media.instructions_for_student: The student will understand that changing to a smaller unit multiplies by 10, 100 or 1,000, changing to a bigger unit divides, and a length can be split into two units.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Double Number Line
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M2.S14.T14.C63.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Far and Near, "Let Us Do" on three double number lines (cm over mm with 1, 7, 15 and 50 cm; m over cm with 1, 4, 10 and 21 m; km over m with 1, 9, 25 and 82 km) and the fourteen conversions (a) to (n). Practice values added: 5 cm, 11 m, 6 km, 1,300 cm, 6,418 cm, 2 km 75 m (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student changes a length between mm, cm, m and km by multiplying or dividing by 10, 100 or 1,000, and splits a length into two units.
- Out of scope: adding or comparing lengths, feet and inches.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A cream wall with two cloth measuring tapes hung one above the other. The top tape is in cm, 0 to 12 cm; the bottom tape is in mm, 0 to 120 mm; their ticks line up. A clear slider (the pointer) stands at 0 and crosses both tapes. A curved arrow from the top tape to the bottom tape carries a box "×10". Three unit chips at the top left: "cm over mm", "m over cm", "km over m".
- Instruction line: "Slide the pointer to 5 cm and read the bottom tape."
- The child is invited to drag the pointer.
2. Scene and Objects
- Tapes: about 90% of the stage width, the unit named in a coloured tab at the left end. The pointer moves on both together and snaps to whole top ticks; two bubbles show its reading on each tape.
- Arrows with boxes, for example "×10" from a top number down to its bottom number. A box or a tick label can be blank ("×___", "___ cm"); tapping it opens a number pad (digits and delete).
- Split tray (Activities 5 and 6): a strip under the tapes with a number tile and a scissors handle that slides between digits.
- Goal chip, for example "5 cm is ___ mm". Pills: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, star, star.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag the pointer; tap a blank and use the pad; tap a unit chip to change the tapes; drag the scissors in the tray.
- Bottom buttons: Hint, Check (becomes Next when done), Reset. Undo is a small back arrow; retry is free.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Slide the pointer to 5 cm and read the bottom tape." Chip: "5 cm is ___ mm". Setup: cm over mm, the arrow "×10" shown. Guess: the child taps "5 mm", "50 mm" or "500 mm" before sliding. Result: the bottom bubble reads 50: "5 cm is 5 × 10 = 50 mm." Help: guided, the arrow and both bubbles.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Slide the pointer to 11 m and read the bottom tape." Chip: "11 m is ___ cm". Setup: m over cm, 0 to 12 m over 0 to 1,200 cm, arrow "×100". Guess: "110 cm", "1,100 cm" or "11,000 cm". Result: "11 m is 11 × 100 = 1,100 cm." Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Slide the pointer to 6 km. Fill the box on the arrow." Chip: "6 km is ___ m". Setup: km over m, the box "×___" empty, no bubbles. Guess: the child taps the multiplier "×10", "×100" or "×1,000". Result: the box and the bottom number fill: "6 km is 6 × 1,000 = 6,000 m." Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Slide the pointer to 1,300 cm on the bottom tape. How many m is that?" Chip: "1,300 cm is ___ m". Setup: m over cm, the arrow turned upward with an empty box "÷___". Guess: "13 m", "130 m" or "13,000 m". Result: "1,300 ÷ 100 = 13 m. Going up to the bigger unit the number gets smaller." Help: independent.
- Activity 5 (guided). Goal line: "Cut 6,418 cm into whole m and the rest." Chip: "6,418 cm is ___ m ___ cm". Setup: the tile "6,418 cm" in the split tray. Guess: the child taps "6 m 418 cm", "64 m 18 cm" or "641 m 8 cm". The child slides the scissors between the hundreds and tens digits: the tile splits into "6,400 cm" and "18 cm"; the child drags "6,400 cm" up to the top tape, where it becomes "64 m". Result: "6,418 cm is 6,400 cm + 18 cm, and 6,400 ÷ 100 = 64 m, so 64 m 18 cm." Help: guided, the cut is shown.
- Activity 6 (independent). Goal line: "Write 2 km 75 m in m." Chip: "2 km 75 m is ___ m". Setup: tiles "2 km" and "75 m". Guess: "275 m", "2,075 m" or "2,750 m". The child drags "2 km" down the arrow, where it becomes "2,000 m", then joins "75 m" to it. Result: "2 km 75 m is 2 × 1,000 + 75 = 2,075 m." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1 (the book's question). Goal line: "Fill in the blanks appropriately in the double number lines given below." Chip: "3 lines". Three tabs. (a) cm over mm. Top: 1 cm, 7 cm, 15 cm, ___, ___, ___, 50 cm. Bottom: 10 mm, ___, ___, 250 mm, 320 mm, 450 mm, ___. Arrows: "×7" on the top tape, "×10" from 1 cm to 10 mm, and two blank boxes "×___", one on the bottom tape between its first two ticks and one on the arrow from the second top tick down to the second bottom tick. Answers: top 25 cm, 32 cm, 45 cm; bottom 70 mm, 150 mm, 500 mm; boxes ×7 and ×10. (b) m over cm. Top: 1 m, 4 m, 10 m, ___, ___, ___, 21 m. Bottom: ___, ___, ___, 1,200 cm, 1,400 cm, 1,700 cm, ___. Arrows "×4" and "×100", two blanks. Answers: top 12 m, 14 m, 17 m; bottom 100 cm, 400 cm, 1,000 cm, 2,100 cm; boxes ×4 and ×100. (c) km over m. Top: 1 km, 9 km, 25 km, ___, ___, ___, 82 km. Bottom: 1,000 m, ___, ___, 41,000 m, 55,000 m, 67,000 m, ___. Arrows "×9" and "×1,000", two blanks. Answers: top 41 km, 55 km, 67 km; bottom 9,000 m, 25,000 m, 82,000 m; boxes ×9 and ×1,000. The ticks are evenly spaced, as in the book. Guess: before filling a line, the child taps which blank is the biggest number. The last bottom blank of (a) shows the unit mm; "50 cm is 50 × 10 = 500 mm." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2 (the book's question). Goal line: "Use your understanding from above to fill in the blanks appropriately." Chip: "14 conversions". Three sets of cards, each card with the book's blanks and a number pad: (a) 4 cm 5 mm = ___ mm; (b) 89 mm = ___ cm ___ mm; (c) 234 cm = ___ mm; (d) 514 mm = ___ cm ___ mm; (e) 6 m 34 cm = ___ cm; (f) 20 m 12 cm = ___ cm; (g) 397 m = ___ cm; (h) 5,792 cm = ___ m ___ cm; (i) 9,108 cm = ___ m ___ cm; (j) 34 km = ___ m; (k) 6,870 m = ___ km ___ m; (l) 10,552 m = ___ km ___ m; (m) 29 km 30 m = ___ m; (n) 32 km 359 m = ___ m. Answers: (a) 45 mm; (b) 8 cm 9 mm; (c) 2,340 mm; (d) 51 cm 4 mm; (e) 634 cm; (f) 2,012 cm; (g) 39,700 cm; (h) 57 m 92 cm; (i) 91 m 8 cm; (j) 34,000 m; (k) 6 km 870 m; (l) 10 km 552 m; (m) 29,030 m; (n) 32,359 m. Guess: for each card, "bigger" or "smaller" for the first blank compared with the first number given. A card turns green when right; the set is done when all its cards are green. Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Sliding one pointer over two tapes shows that one length has two numbers, and that the bottom number is always the top number times 10, 100 or 1,000. The arrows show the same multiplier at every tick.
- Rules in the child's words: 10 mm make 1 cm, 100 cm make 1 m, 1,000 m make 1 km; going down, multiply; going up, divide; to split, take out the whole bigger units and keep the rest.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the blank and the goal chip turn green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick and Next unlocks. Confetti only on the end screen.
- Wrong (every case): red strip, a small shake, ONE friendly line; no score; try again.
- 5 cm as "500 mm" -> "1 cm is 10 mm, not 100 mm. Look at the ×10 arrow." 11 m as "110 cm" -> "1 m is 100 cm, not 10 cm." 6 km as "600 m" -> "1 km is 1,000 m, not 100 m." The arrow pulses.
- Divided going down -> "Going down to the smaller unit the number gets bigger. Multiply." Multiplied going up -> "Going up to the bigger unit the number gets smaller. Divide."
- 2 km 75 m as "275 m" -> "2 km is 2,000 m. Then add 75 m." As "2,750 m" -> "75 m is 75 m, not 750 m."
- A wrong cut in the tray -> "6,000 cm is 60 m, but 418 cm is left, and that is more than 100 cm. Cut so that less than 100 cm is left."
- A wrong box -> "×7 goes with the jump from 1 to 7 on the top tape. The bottom tape jumps the same way." A wrong blank -> "Going down the multiplier is 10, so multiply the top number by 10." (own numbers).
- Hints (3 levels): (1) "Which unit is on the top tape and which is on the bottom tape? Which one is bigger?" (2) the arrow lights up with its multiplier and the pointer slides to a nearby tick to compare both numbers; (3) "Multiply the top number by that multiplier to get the bottom number. To go up, divide." and the blank is half filled.
- Edge cases: a zero in the middle (2 km 75 m is 2,075 m); the book's ticks are evenly spaced although the numbers are not.
7. Ending
- Star 1 is done when the three lines are right; Star 2 when all 14 cards are green.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "10 mm make 1 cm, 100 cm make 1 m, 1,000 m make 1 km." "Going down to a smaller unit, multiply. Going up, divide." "To split a length, take out the whole bigger units and keep the rest." Think and talk: "Why is the number for the same length bigger in mm than in cm?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Photo of a cream wall. Code-drawn: the two tapes (with a cloth texture), tick marks, pointer, arrows, boxes, number pad, tray, scissors, tiles. Language: simple English; units beside every number.

content.text:
Worked example: Change 6 cm to mm, 9 m to cm and 8 km to m (practice values).
1. Going from a bigger unit to a smaller unit, multiply.
2. 6 cm to mm: 1 cm = 10 mm, so 6 × 10 = 60 mm.
3. 9 m to cm: 1 m = 100 cm, so 9 × 100 = 900 cm.
4. 8 km to m: 1 km = 1,000 m, so 8 × 1,000 = 8,000 m.
5. Check by dividing back: 60 ÷ 10 = 6, 900 ÷ 100 = 9 and 8,000 ÷ 1,000 = 8.
Answer: 6 cm = 60 mm, 9 m = 900 cm and 8 km = 8,000 m

concepts.concept_name: Changing Between mm, cm, m and km

content.text:
1. Predict first: how would you write 7,305 cm in m and cm?
2. Take out the part that is a whole number of m: 7,305 cm = 7,300 cm + 5 cm. What is left stays in cm.
3. 7,300 cm = 7,300 ÷ 100 = 73 m, so 7,305 cm = 73 m 5 cm.
4. Your maths book shows the same idea: 89 mm = 80 mm + 9 mm = 8 cm 9 mm, and 5,792 cm = 5,700 cm + 92 cm = 57 m 92 cm.
5. To go the other way, change the bigger unit to the smaller unit and add the rest: 3 m 7 cm = 300 cm + 7 cm = 307 cm.
6. Rule: split off the part that is a whole number of the bigger unit and keep the rest in the smaller unit.

content.text:
1. The top line is in cm and the bottom line is in mm. Going down, multiply by $10$, because $1\text{ cm} = 10\text{ mm}$.
2. The arrow $\times 7$ on the top line goes from $1\text{ cm}$ to $7\text{ cm}$, so the arrow on the bottom line from $10\text{ mm}$ to the next blank is also $\times 7$: $10 \times 7 = 70\text{ mm}$.
3. $7\text{ cm} = 7 \times 10 = 70\text{ mm}$, and the box on the arrow from the top line to the bottom line is $\times 10$. $15\text{ cm} = 15 \times 10 = 150\text{ mm}$.
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution]
4. Going up, divide by $10$: $250 \div 10 = 25\text{ cm}$, $320 \div 10 = 32\text{ cm}$ and $450 \div 10 = 45\text{ cm}$.
5. $50\text{ cm} = 50 \times 10 = 500\text{ mm}$. Your maths book prints m under this tick, but $50\text{ cm}$ is $500\text{ mm}$, which is also half a metre.
6. Check: $7 \times 10 = 70$ and $70 \div 10 = 7$.
Answer: Top: $25\text{ cm}$, $32\text{ cm}$, $45\text{ cm}$. Bottom: $70\text{ mm}$, $150\text{ mm}$, $500\text{ mm}$. Boxes: $\times 7$, $\times 10$
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution (continued)]

media.title: Length Columns

tool_config.idea: Add and subtract lengths given in two units in a column for each unit, with exchange chips for regrouping: 1 km = 1,000 m and 1 m = 100 cm.
tool_config.title: Length Columns
tool_config.screen: The cutting table of the village weaving centre, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation, with a chart of two columns on the wall. The chart is the largest object on screen: columns headed km and m (or m and cm), rows for the first length, the second length and the answer, and a plus or minus sign on the left. Number tiles sit in the cells. Exchange chips wait beside the chart: a chip marked 1 km turns into 1,000 m and back, and a chip marked 1 m turns into 100 cm and back. A check strip below changes the whole sum to the smaller unit as a second way. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type with progress dots under it. Controls: tap a cell and type a number; drag an exchange chip across a column border; tap Add or Subtract; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the cells of this card), Reset (restores the table), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the sum in the smaller unit, the carried or exchanged amount, and a card number out of 7.
feedback: Typing in a cell shows the number in its column. If a cell holds more than a full bigger unit, the tool says, for example: 1,700 m is more than 1,000 m, so exchange 1,000 m for 1 km.
An exchange chip moves across the column border and the numbers change together, for example 1 km becomes 1,000 m.
In a subtraction, if the bottom number is bigger than the top number in a column, the tool says: You cannot take 40 cm from 0 cm. Exchange 1 m for 100 cm first.
The check strip changes the whole sum to the smaller unit and shows that both ways give the same length.
A wrong answer slides back with a clue such as: Did you exchange 1 m as 100 cm and not as 10 cm?
tool_config.done_when: All five practice cards are solved, the two examples are worked, and the three word problems and the seven pairs are answered.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): add 2 km 900 m and 1 km 800 m in the km and m columns. Answer: 900 m + 800 m = 1,700 m, carry 1 km and write 700 m, and 2 km + 1 km + 1 km = 4 km, so 4 km 700 m.
Card 2 (practice values): add 5 m 60 cm and 3 m 70 cm in the m and cm columns. Answer: 60 cm + 70 cm = 130 cm, carry 1 m and write 30 cm, and 5 m + 3 m + 1 m = 9 m, so 9 m 30 cm.
Card 3 (practice values): subtract 3 m 40 cm from 9 m. Answer: exchange 1 m for 100 cm, so 9 m becomes 8 m 100 cm, and 8 m 100 cm − 3 m 40 cm = 5 m 60 cm.
Card 4 (practice values): subtract 2 km 600 m from 5 km 200 m. Answer: exchange 1 km for 1,000 m, so 5 km 200 m becomes 4 km 1,200 m, and 4 km 1,200 m − 2 km 600 m = 2 km 600 m.
Card 5: check card 4 by changing to m. Answer: 5,200 − 2,600 = 2,600 m = 2 km 600 m.

Challenge: 'Saji saw on his smartphone that he walked 3 km 450 m in the morning and another 4 km 650 m in the evening. How much did he walk in the whole day?' and 'They need 63 m of cable for this purpose. They used 16 m 75 cm cable in the first room. What is the length of the cable left?' Answer: 8 km 100 m, and 46 m 25 cm.

Challenge: 'Rani has two red coloured ribbon rolls, one of length 3 m 75 cm and another 2 m 25 cm long. How much ribbon does she have?'; 'The distance from Bhopal to Sanchi is 48 km 700 m ... 17 km 900 m away from Bhopal. How far is Sanchi from the waterfall?'; 'The first section covers 2 km 300 m and the second section covers 2 km 650 m'; and 'Circle the bigger length and find the difference' for the seven pairs. Answer: 6 m; 30 km 800 m; 4 km 950 m; and the pairs: (a) 11 mm, 1 mm; (b) 26 mm, 6 mm; (c) 201 mm, 1 mm; (d) 1,020 mm, 20 mm; (e) 245 cm, 45 cm; (f) 6 km, 322 m; (g) 6 km 1,480 m, 1 m.

hint_ladder.text: Which two units are in the table? Put each length into its own columns.
Start with the smaller unit. Can the answer in that column be changed to a bigger unit?
1 km = 1,000 m and 1 m = 100 cm. Exchange one bigger unit for the smaller unit when you subtract, or carry it when you add.
The tool does the exchange with the chip and shows the new numbers in both columns.

media.instructions_for_student: The student will understand that lengths are added and subtracted unit by unit, regrouping 1 km as 1,000 m and 1 m as 100 cm.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Length Columns
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M3.S16.T16.C78.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Far and Near, "Adding and Subtracting Lengths": Example 1 (Saji, 3 km 450 m and 4 km 650 m), Example 2 (the cable, 63 m and 16 m 75 cm), questions 1 to 3 (Rani; Bhopal to Sanchi; Gulmarg Gondola) and question 4 (seven pairs). Practice values added: 5 m 60 cm + 3 m 70 cm, 8 m − 2 m 35 cm, 6 km 300 m − 2 km 800 m (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student adds and subtracts lengths given in two units in a column for each unit, regrouping 1 km as 1,000 m and 1 m as 100 cm.
- Out of scope: multiplying or dividing lengths, feet and inches.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A pale wooden counting board (photo). A chart of two columns fills the stage: headed "m" and "cm", rows "Length 1", "Length 2" and "Answer", a "+" sign at the left. A story strip at the top shows two ribbon rolls (photo) with cards "5 m 60 cm" and "3 m 70 cm". Two chips wait beside the chart: "1 m" and "1 km".
- Instruction line: "Tap each length to put it in the chart."
- The child is invited to tap the first length card.
2. Scene and Objects
- Chart: about 70% of the stage, cells large enough for a finger, with a small "+1" slot above the bigger-unit column for a regrouped chip.
- Story strip: a photo cut-out for each problem (ribbon rolls, a path, a cable coil, a road map, a cable car) with the length cards; tapping a card drops its parts into their columns.
- Regroup chips: a gold "1 km" chip that turns into "1,000 m" and a gold "1 m" chip that turns into "100 cm", and back. A cell takes a number from a small number pad.
- Check strip: opened by "Check in the smaller unit"; shows both lengths in the smaller unit and the sum or difference.
- Goal chip, for example "5 m 60 cm + 3 m 70 cm". Pills: 1, 2, 3, star, star, star.
3. Main Interaction
- Tap a length card to fill the chart. Tap an answer cell to type its number. Drag a chip across the column border to regroup: a full 100 cm leaves the cm cell as a "1 m" chip and lands in the "+1" slot; for a subtraction a "1 m" chip leaves the top m cell and lands in the cm cell as 100 cm. Tap + or − chips to choose the sign in word problems.
- Bottom buttons: Hint, Check (becomes Next when done), Reset. Undo is a small back arrow; retry is free.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Add the two ribbons. Start with the cm." Chip: "5 m 60 cm + 3 m 70 cm". Setup: m and cm columns, the first cell guide lit. Guess: the child taps "8 m 130 cm", "9 m 30 cm" or "8 m 30 cm". The child types 130 in the cm cell, drags 100 cm out as a "1 m" chip, types 9 in the m cell. Result: "60 cm + 70 cm = 130 cm, which is 1 m 30 cm. 5 m + 3 m + 1 m is 9 m, so 9 m 30 cm." Help: guided.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Take away 2 m 35 cm from 8 m." Chip: "8 m − 2 m 35 cm". Setup: top row "8 m 0 cm", bottom row "2 m 35 cm", "−" sign. Guess: the child taps "6 m 65 cm", "5 m 65 cm" or "6 m 35 cm". The child sees that 0 cm has no 35 cm to give, drags a "1 m" chip from the top m cell into the cm cell (it becomes 100 cm and the m cell reads 7), then types 65 and 5. Result: "8 m is 7 m 100 cm. 100 cm − 35 cm = 65 cm and 7 m − 2 m = 5 m, so 5 m 65 cm." Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Take away 2 km 800 m from 6 km 300 m. Then check it in m." Chip: "6 km 300 m − 2 km 800 m". Setup: km and m columns, no guide. Guess: "4 km 500 m", "3 km 500 m" or "4 km 100 m". The child regroups and fills the answer, then opens the check strip and types the m numbers. Result: "5 km 1,300 m − 2 km 800 m is 3 km 500 m. Check: 6,300 − 2,800 = 3,500 m, which is 3 km 500 m." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1 (the book's examples). Goal line: the book's question of each tab. Chip: "2 examples". Two tabs: (a) "Saji saw on his smartphone that he walked 3 km 450 m in the morning and another 4 km 650 m in the evening. How much did he walk in the whole day? How would you solve this problem?" (b) "Electricians are changing the cables in a house. They need 63 m of cable for this purpose. They used 16 m 75 cm cable in the first room. What is the length of the cable left?" The child taps + or − first (guess), fills the chart and regroups. Results: "450 m + 650 m = 1,100 m, which is 1 km 100 m. 3 km + 4 km + 1 km is 8 km, so 8 km 100 m. In m: 3,450 + 4,650 = 8,100 m." and "63 m is 62 m 100 cm. 100 cm − 75 cm = 25 cm and 62 m − 16 m = 46 m, so 46 m 25 cm." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2 (the book's questions). Goal line: the book's question of each tab. Chip: "3 problems". Three tabs: (a) "Rani has two red coloured ribbon rolls, one of length 3 m 75 cm and another 2 m 25 cm long. How much ribbon does she have?" (b) "The distance from Bhopal to Sanchi is 48 km 700 m. Bhadbhada Ghat waterfall is on the way, and 17 km 900 m away from Bhopal. How far is Sanchi from the waterfall?" (c) "Gulmarg Gondola in Gulmarg, Kashmir is the second longest and second highest cable car in the world. It is divided into two sections. The first section covers 2 km 300 m and the second section covers 2 km 650 m. What is the total distance covered by the cable car?" The child taps + or − first, fills the chart and regroups. Answers: (a) 6 m; (b) 30 km 800 m; (c) 4 km 950 m. Result for (a): "75 cm + 25 cm = 100 cm, which is 1 m. 3 m + 2 m + 1 m is 6 m." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3 (the book's question). Goal line: "Circle the bigger length and find the difference." Chip: "7 pairs". Seven tabs: (a) "11 mm and 1 cm"; (b) "26 mm and 2 cm"; (c) "20 cm and 201 mm"; (d) "1,020 mm and 1 m"; (e) "2 m and 245 cm"; (f) "5,678 m and 6 km"; (g) "6 km 1,480 m and 7 km 479 m". The child taps the bigger card (the circle, a guess), drags the bigger-unit chip into the chart where it turns into the smaller unit, types the difference and Check. Answers (bigger, difference): (a) 11 mm, 1 mm; (b) 26 mm, 6 mm; (c) 201 mm, 1 mm; (d) 1,020 mm, 20 mm; (e) 245 cm, 45 cm; (f) 6 km, 322 m; (g) 6 km 1,480 m, 1 m. Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Each unit keeps its own column; a full 1,000 m or 100 cm leaves a column as a bigger-unit chip; to subtract, a bigger unit is first broken into the smaller unit. The check strip shows the same answer in one unit.
- Rules in the child's words: add like units, then regroup the smaller unit into the bigger one; to subtract, regroup 1 m as 100 cm or 1 km as 1,000 m first; check by changing both to the smaller unit.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the cell and the goal chip turn green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick and Next unlocks. Confetti only on the end screen.
- Wrong (every case): red strip, a small shake, ONE friendly line; no score; try again.
- Cell above the full unit (for example 1,300 m left in the m cell) -> "1,300 m is more than 1,000 m. Regroup 1,000 m as 1 km." The cell and the chip pulse.
- 1 m regrouped as 10 cm -> "1 m is 100 cm, not 10 cm."
- Subtracting with a smaller top cell -> "You cannot take 35 cm from 0 cm. Regroup 1 m as 100 cm first." The top m cell pulses.
- Forgot the regrouped chip -> "Did you add the 1 km that you regrouped?" The "+1" slot pulses.
- Wrong sign in a word problem -> "The waterfall is on the way to Sanchi, so it is less far from Sanchi. Subtract." (each problem has its own line).
- Wrong "bigger" in (g) -> "6 km 1,480 m has more than 1,000 m in the m place. Change both to m and look again."
- Hints (3 levels): (1) "Which two units are in the table? Put each length into its own columns." (2) the smaller unit's column lights up and the regroup chip pulses; (3) "1 km is 1,000 m and 1 m is 100 cm. Regroup one bigger unit into the smaller unit when you subtract." and the chip does the regrouping.
- Edge cases: a column that ends exactly on the full unit (75 cm + 25 cm is 100 cm, leaving 0 cm: write "6 m"); a top cell that is 0; pairs that differ by 1 mm or 1 m.
7. Ending
- Star 1 is done when 8 km 100 m and 46 m 25 cm are right; Star 2 when 6 m, 30 km 800 m and 4 km 950 m are right; Star 3 when all seven pairs are right.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "Add like units, then regroup the smaller unit into the bigger one." "To subtract, regroup 1 m as 100 cm or 1 km as 1,000 m first." "Check by changing both lengths to the smaller unit." Think and talk: "Why do we regroup 1 m as 100 cm and not as 10 cm?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Photos: pale wood board; ribbon rolls; a path; a cable coil; a road map; a cable car. Code-drawn: chart, tiles, gold chips, number pad, check strip. Language: simple English; "regroup".

video_script.why: Show how to add lengths given in two units, by like units or by changing to the smaller unit, and regroup.
source: Sonu walked 2 km 700 m to the market and 1 km 800 m back by
video_script.status: placeholder: the script and the video are made in the media folders

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: Sonu walked 2 km 700 m to the market and 1 km 800 m back by another road. How far did he walk in all? Add like units. Add the km: 2 km + 1 km = 3 km. Add the m: 700 m + 800 m = 1,500 m. 1,500 m is more than 1,000 m, so regroup: 1,500 m = 1 km 500 m. Then 3 km + 1 km 500 m = 4 km 500 m. Or change both to m and add: 2 km 700 m = 2,700 m and 1 km 800 m = 1,800 m, and 2,700 + 1,800 = 4,500 m = 4 km 500 m. When the numbers are easy, such as 200, 250, 400, 500 or 750, you can add in your head. When they are not, write the two lengths in a column, one unit in each column, and regroup: 1 km = 1,000 m and 1 m = 100 cm. Lengths add just like numbers, but each unit keeps its own column. 1. Add like units. Add the m: $3\text{ m} + 2\text{ m} = 5\text{ m}$.

Answer: $6\text{ m}$

5. $(d)$: $1\text{ m} = 1,000\text{ mm}$. $1,020\text{ mm}$ is more than $1,000\text{ mm}$. The difference is $1,020 - 1,000 = 20\text{ mm}$.
6. Check: $20\text{ mm} = 2\text{ cm}$, and $1,000 + 20 = 1,020$.
Answer: Bigger, difference: $(a)$: $11\text{ mm}$, $1\text{ mm}$; $(b)$: $26\text{ mm}$, $6\text{ mm}$; $(c)$: $201\text{ mm}$, $1\text{ mm}$; $(d)$: $1,020\text{ mm}$, $20\text{ mm}$

media.title: Cut and Share

tool_config.idea: Multiply and divide a length given in two units by working on each unit and then regrouping: copies of a length laid end to end give so many m and so many cm, and a road shared into equal days gives each day its km and m.
tool_config.title: Cut and Share
tool_config.screen: The cutting table of the village weaving centre with a roll of cloth and a road strip beside it, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A strip of cloth of a chosen length in m and cm lies on a tape, and it is the largest object on screen. A Make copies stepper lays copies of the strip end to end along the tape, and two piles collect the parts: a m pile and a cm pile. An exchange chip turns 100 cm into 1 m. For division, a road bar of a chosen length in km and m has a Share into stepper that fills equal day boxes, each with a km part and a m part, and a leftover chip turns 1 km into 1,000 m when the km do not share equally. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type with progress dots under it. Controls: the Make copies stepper; drag the parts of a strip into the m pile and the cm pile; tap the exchange chip; the Share into stepper; type an answer into a box; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the piles of this card), Reset (restores the roll and the road), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the number of copies, the m pile and the cm pile, the total after the exchange, and a card number out of 7.
feedback: Each copy lands at the end of the last one along the tape, and the piles count the parts: for example 5 copies give 15 m in the m pile and 100 cm in the cm pile.
When the cm pile reaches 100 cm or more, the tool says: 100 cm make 1 m. Tap the chip to change them.
For a road, each day box shows its km and its m. If the km do not share equally, the tool says: Change the whole road to m first, then share.
A wrong total slides back with a clue such as: Did you multiply the cm as well as the m?
After the exchange the tool shows the total in one line, for example 16 m, and checks it against the same length in cm.
tool_config.done_when: All five practice cards are solved, and the shirts, Anita's thread and its cost, and the road are answered.

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): lay 5 copies of a strip of 3 m 20 cm and sort the parts. Answer: 5 × 3 m = 15 m and 5 × 20 cm = 100 cm = 1 m, so 16 m.
Card 2 (practice values): lay 6 copies of a strip of 1 m 50 cm and sort the parts. Answer: 6 × 1 m = 6 m and 6 × 50 cm = 300 cm = 3 m, so 9 m.
Card 3 (practice values): lay 8 copies of a strip of 2 m 25 cm and sort the parts. Answer: 8 × 2 m = 16 m and 8 × 25 cm = 200 cm = 2 m, so 18 m.
Card 4 (practice values): share a road of 24 km 800 m into 4 equal days. Answer: 24 km divided by 4 is 6 km and 800 m divided by 4 is 200 m, so 6 km 200 m a day.
Card 5 (practice values): share a road of 7 km 200 m into 4 equal days. 7 km does not share equally among 4, so change the whole road to m. Answer: 7,200 ÷ 4 = 1,800 m = 1 km 800 m a day.

Challenge: 'We need a 1 m 80 cm cloth to make a shirt for a 10 year old child. How much cloth will be needed to make shirts for 20 such children?' Then: 'Anita is making an embroidery on the border of a sari. She needs a 1 m long thread to embroider a 50 cm sari. How much thread would she need for a 5 m sari border? A 1 m long thread costs ₹50. How much money will be needed to buy the thread?' Answer: 20 × 1 m = 20 m and 20 × 80 cm = 1,600 cm = 16 m, so 36 m; the 5 m border is 500 cm and 500 ÷ 50 = 10, so 10 m of thread, and 10 × 50 = ₹500.

Challenge: 'A road 12 km 600 m long is being laid in a town. The workers lay an equal length of road each day, and complete the work in 6 days. How much road laying work is done on each day?' Answer: 12 km divided by 6 is 2 km and 600 m divided by 6 is 100 m, so 2 km 100 m a day.

The tool lays the pieces or shares the road and shows each pile: read the total.

media.instructions_for_student: The student will understand that a length is multiplied or divided part by part with regrouping, and that the price of 1 m is the price shared by the number of metres.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Cut and Share
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M3.S19.T19.C96.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Far and Near, "Multiplying and Dividing Lengths": Example 3 (20 shirts of 1 m 80 cm), the bag cloth at ₹100 for 5 m with its double number line, Anita's thread (5 m border, 50 cm, ₹50) and the road of 12 km 600 m in 6 days. Practice values added: 3 m 20 cm × 5, 24 km 800 m ÷ 4, 7 km 200 m ÷ 4, ₹72 for 6 m (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student multiplies and divides a length given in two units by working on each unit and regrouping, and finds the price of 1 m by sharing the price equally.
- Out of scope: adding or subtracting two different lengths, mm.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A wooden cutting table (photo) with a cloth roll at the left and a tape along its edge. A cloth strip lies on the tape with a card "3 m 20 cm". Under the table edge a stepper "Copies: 1" with + and −, and two empty trays, "m pile" and "cm pile".
- Instruction line: "Make 5 copies of the strip and lay them end to end."
- The child is invited to tap + on the stepper.
2. Scene and Objects
- Strip: a cloth strip drawn to scale with its length card; copies lay end to end as the stepper goes up. Goal chip, for example "5 × 3 m 20 cm". Pills: 1, 2, 3, 4, star, star, star.
- Piles: a "m pile" and a "cm pile" (trays). The child drags the m part and the cm part of each copy (or of all, in one drag) into them. Dropping the cm pile on the m pile turns every full 100 cm into 1 m.
- Road board: a road bar of a chosen length in km and m on a map board, a stepper "Days: 1" and day boxes, each with a km part and a m part.
- Price shelf: cloth and ribbon rolls (photo) with a price tag, a ₹ note that splits into equal piles, and a double number line.
3. Main Interaction
- Stepper + and −: copies or days. Drag parts into trays or day boxes. A number pad takes answers; chips take guesses.
- Bottom buttons: Hint, Check (becomes Next when done), Reset. Undo is a small back arrow; retry is free.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Make 5 copies of the strip and lay them end to end." Chip: "5 × 3 m 20 cm". Setup: strip "3 m 20 cm", the two piles labelled. Guess: "8 m", "16 m" or "160 m". The child sets 5 copies, drags the 5 m parts into the m pile and the 5 cm parts into the cm pile, then drops the cm pile on the m pile. Result: "5 × 3 m = 15 m and 5 × 20 cm = 100 cm, which is 1 m. So 16 m." Help: guided.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Share the road into 4 equal days." Chip: "24 km 800 m ÷ 4". Setup: a road of 24 km 800 m, 4 empty day boxes. Guess: "6 km 200 m", "6 km 800 m" or "20 km 800 m". The child drags the 24 km into the boxes, then the 800 m. Result: "24 km ÷ 4 = 6 km and 800 m ÷ 4 = 200 m, so 6 km 200 m a day." Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Share the road into 4 equal days." Chip: "7 km 200 m ÷ 4". Setup: a road of 7 km 200 m. Guess: "1 km 800 m", "1 km 50 m" or "1 km 200 m". The 7 km will not share equally, so the child taps the road to change it to 7,200 m and shares. Result: "7 km is not shared equally by 4. 7,200 ÷ 4 = 1,800 m, which is 1 km 800 m." Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (guided). Goal line: "Ribbon costs ₹72 for 6 m. How much is 1 m? And 15 m?" Chip: "₹72 for 6 m". Setup: a ₹72 note beside 6 metre slots. Guess: "₹12", "₹66" or "₹432". The ₹72 splits into 6 equal piles: "72 ÷ 6 = ₹12." Then the child picks the cost of 15 m from "₹180", "₹87" or "₹90": "15 × 12 = ₹180." Help: guided.
- Star Challenge 1 (the book's questions). Goal line: the book's question of each part. Chip: "Shirts and thread". (a) "We need a 1 m 80 cm cloth to make a shirt for a 10 year old child. How much cloth will be needed to make shirts for 20 such children?" The child sets 20 copies and sorts the parts. Result: "20 × 1 m = 20 m and 20 × 80 cm = 1,600 cm, which is 16 m. 20 m + 16 m = 36 m." (b) "Anita is making an embroidery on the border of a sari. She needs a 1 m long thread to embroider a 50 cm sari. How much thread would she need for a 5 m sari border? A 1 m long thread costs ₹50. How much money will be needed to buy the thread?" A photo of a sari border 5 m long shows in 50 cm parts; "Add a 1 m thread" lays one thread over the next 50 cm. Guess: "5 m", "10 m" or "50 m". The child adds threads until the border is covered, then taps the cost from "₹250", "₹500" or "₹5,000". Result: "5 m is 500 cm and 500 ÷ 50 = 10, so 10 m of thread. 10 × ₹50 = ₹500." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2 (the book's questions). Goal line: the book's question of each part. Chip: "Price of cloth". (a) "A shop sells cloth for making bags at ₹100 for 5 m. How much money is needed to buy a 1 m cloth?" Guess: "₹5", "₹20" or "₹500"; the ₹100 note splits into 5 equal piles. Result: "100 ÷ 5 = ₹20." (b) "Now, use the double number line to find the cost of the cloth or the length of cloth that we can buy at a particular cost." Top line: 5 m, 10 m, 20 m, 40 m, ___ m. Bottom line: ₹100, ₹___, ₹___, ₹___, ₹2000. Four boxes "×___": 5 m to 10 m on the top line, 5 m to ₹100, ₹100 to the next amount, and 10 m to the next amount. The child fills the blanks with the number pad. Answers: ₹200, ₹400, ₹800; 100 m; boxes ×2, ×20, ×2, ×20. The ticks are evenly spaced, as in the book. Result: "5 m to 10 m is ×2, so ₹100 to ₹200 is ×2. 1 m costs ₹20, so m to ₹ is ×20. ₹2000 ÷ ₹20 = 100 m." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3 (the book's question). Goal line: "A road 12 km 600 m long is being laid in a town. The workers lay an equal length of road each day, and complete the work in 6 days. How much road laying work is done on each day?" Chip: "12 km 600 m ÷ 6". The child sets 6 days and shares. Guess: "2 km 100 m", "2 km 10 m" or "2 km 600 m". Result: "12 km ÷ 6 = 2 km and 600 m ÷ 6 = 100 m, so 2 km 100 m a day." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- The two piles show that a length is two parts and each part is multiplied or shared on its own; 100 cm leaves the cm pile as 1 m. Equal piles of money show that the price of 1 m is the price shared among the metres, and the double number line moves both lines by the same multiplier.
- Rules in the child's words: break the length into two units, work on each, then regroup; the price of 1 m is the price ÷ the number of metres.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the pile or box and the goal chip turn green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick and Next unlocks. Confetti only on the end screen.
- Wrong (every case): red strip, a small shake, ONE friendly line; no score; try again.
- Only the m part multiplied -> "You multiplied the m but not the cm. Every copy has cm too. Look at the cm pile." The cm pile pulses.
- 100 cm or more left in the cm pile -> "100 cm make 1 m. Drop the cm pile on the m pile." 1 m as 10 cm -> "1 m is 100 cm, not 10 cm."
- The km do not share equally -> "7 km does not share equally among 4 days. Change the whole road to m first." The road pulses.
- A part left out of a day box -> "Did you share the m part too? The 800 m also goes into the 4 boxes."
- ₹100 or ₹500 for 1 m -> "₹100 buys 5 m, not 1 m. Share the ₹100 equally among the 5 metres." A wrong box -> "5 m to 10 m is ×2, so the price also jumps ×2." or "1 m costs ₹20, so from m to rupees multiply by 20."
- Anita, 5 m of thread -> "1 m of thread covers only 50 cm of border. How many 50 cm are in the 5 m border?" The uncovered border pulses. ₹250 -> "You need 10 m of thread, not 5 m."
- Hints (3 levels): (1) "How many copies or how many days? What are the two parts of the length?" (2) the two parts light up in two colours; (3) "Multiply or share the m part and the cm part separately. If the cm pile has 100 or more, change 100 cm to 1 m. If the km do not share equally, change the road to m." and the pieces are laid for the child.
- Edge cases: 100 cm exactly makes 1 m with nothing left over (Activity 1); the 5 m border is covered by exactly 10 threads.
7. Ending
- Star 1 is done when 36 m, 10 m and ₹500 are right; Star 2 when ₹20 and the whole double number line are right; Star 3 when 2 km 100 m is right.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "Break the length into m and cm, work on each, then regroup." "The price of 1 m is the price divided by the number of metres." "To divide a length, divide each part, or change it to the smaller unit." Think and talk: "Why does 20 × 80 cm give 16 m?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Photos: cutting table; cloth and ribbon rolls; sari border; ₹ note; map board. Flat drawings: Rani, Anita. Code-drawn: strips, tape, trays, steppers, road bar, boxes, double number line. Language: simple English.

Worked example: A shop sells ribbon at ₹90 for 3 m (practice values). What does 1 m cost? What do 9 m cost? How many m can you buy for ₹300?
1. Share the ₹90 equally among the 3 m: 90 ÷ 3 = ₹30 for 1 m.
2. 9 m is 3 times 3 m, so the price is 3 times ₹90: 3 × 90 = ₹270.
3. Or 9 m at ₹30 for each metre: 9 × 30 = ₹270.
4. For ₹300, divide by the price of 1 m: 300 ÷ 30 = 10 m.
5. Check: 10 × 30 = ₹300.
Answer: 1 m costs ₹30, 9 m cost ₹270, and ₹300 buys 10 m

content.publication_text: We need a $1\text{ m } 80\text{ cm}$ cloth to make a shirt for a $10$ year old child. How much cloth will be needed to make shirts for $20$ such children?

content.text:
1. Break the length into m and cm: $1\text{ m } 80\text{ cm}$ is $1\text{ m}$ and $80\text{ cm}$. Multiply each part by $20$.
2. $20 \times 1\text{ m} = 20\text{ m}$.
3. $20 \times 80\text{ cm} = 1,600\text{ cm}$.
4. $1,600\text{ cm} = 16\text{ m}$, because $1,600 \div 100 = 16$.
5. Add: $20\text{ m} + 16\text{ m} = 36\text{ m}$.
6. Check in cm: $20 \times 180 = 3,600\text{ cm} = 36\text{ m}$.
Answer: $36\text{ m}$

content.publication_text: A shop sells cloth for making bags at ₹$100$ for $5\text{ m}$. How much money is needed to buy a $1\text{ m}$ cloth?

content.text:
1. ₹$100$ buys $5\text{ m}$ of cloth. To find the price of $1\text{ m}$, share the ₹$100$ equally among the $5\text{ m}$.
2. $100 \div 5 =$ ₹$20$.
3. So a $1\text{ m}$ cloth costs ₹$20$.
4. Check: $5 \times 20 =$ ₹$100$.
Answer: ₹$20$

content.text:
1. The thread is $1\text{ m}$ for every $50\text{ cm}$ of the sari border. First change the $5\text{ m}$ border to cm: $5 \times 100 = 500\text{ cm}$.
2. How many pieces of $50\text{ cm}$ are in $500\text{ cm}$? $500 \div 50 = 10$.
3. Each $50\text{ cm}$ of border needs $1\text{ m}$ of thread, so $10 \times 1\text{ m} = 10\text{ m}$ of thread.
4. The thread costs ₹$50$ for $1\text{ m}$, so $10\text{ m}$ cost $10 \times 50 =$ ₹$500$.
5. Check: $10\text{ m}$ of thread for $500\text{ cm}$ of border, and $10 \times 50 = 500$.
Answer: $10\text{ m}$ of thread, costing ₹$500$

1. Change the road to m: $12\text{ km } 600\text{ m} = 12 \times 1,000 + 600 = 12,600\text{ m}$.
2. The same length is laid each day for $6$ days: $12,600 \div 6 = 2,100\text{ m}$.
3. Change back: $2,100\text{ m} = 2,000\text{ m} + 100\text{ m} = 2\text{ km } 100\text{ m}$.
4. Another way: $12\text{ km}$ divided by $6$ is $2\text{ km}$, and $600\text{ m}$ divided by $6$ is $100\text{ m}$.
5. Check: $6 \times 2,100 = 12,600\text{ m}$.
Answer: $2\text{ km } 100\text{ m}$ each day

tool_config.idea: Read a height in feet and inches (12 inches = 1 foot) and find the tallest in a list by changing every height to inches.
tool_config.title: Height Chart
tool_config.screen: The wall of the village weaving centre with a tall wooden height chart, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The chart is the largest object on screen: a tall wooden scale with a foot mark and 12 inch marks in every foot on one edge and a cm scale on the other edge. A child figure stands against it with a draggable mark at the top of the head. A read-out beside the chart says the height in feet and inches and in inches only, for example 4 feet 6 inches = 54 inches, and a note says 1 inch = 2 cm 5 mm and 1 foot = 12 inches = 30 cm. A class list on a board next to the chart has rows where the student types feet and inches, and a Find the tallest button sorts them. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type with progress dots under it. Controls: drag the head mark up or down (it snaps to an inch mark); type feet and inches into a list row; tap Find the tallest; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the row being worked), Reset (restores the chart and the list), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: feet and inches, inches, cm, the sorted list, and a card number out of 6.
feedback: The head mark snaps to an inch mark and the read-out shows feet and inches, inches, and cm, for example: 4 feet 6 inches is 4 × 12 + 6 = 54 inches.
If the inches typed are 12 or more, the tool says: 12 inches make 1 foot. Change them to feet.
Find the tallest sorts the heights by inches and shows the numbers, so that the student sees why 4 feet 7 inches is more than 4 feet 5 inches.
A wrong inch count slides back with a clue such as: 1 foot is 12 inches, not 10 inches.
In the book's task the tool keeps the student's list on the board and says how many students are in it.

media.instructions_for_student: The student will understand that 1 foot is 12 inches, so feet and inches change to inches by multiplying the feet by 12 and adding the inches.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Height Chart
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M3.S24.T24.C116.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Far and Near, "Let Us Explore" on feet and inches (1 inch is 2 cm 5 mm; 1 foot is 12 inches or 30 cm; find how many cm and mm make 1 inch) and "Measure Your Height" (mark your height, measure it in feet and inches, find the tallest student). Practice values added: 5 feet 2 inches, 45 inches, 2 feet, 4 feet 1 inch, 3 feet 11 inches, 4 feet 2 inches, and a practice class of 4 feet 3 inches, 4 feet 7 inches and 4 feet 5 inches (developer only).
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student reads a height in feet and inches, changes it to inches using 12 inches in 1 foot, and finds the tallest of several heights.
- Out of scope: adding or subtracting heights, other units of length.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A tall wooden height chart hung on a cream wall (photo), the largest object on the stage. Its left edge has foot marks "1 foot" to "6 feet", each foot cut into 12 inch marks; its right edge is a cm scale. A flat-drawn child stands against it with a round pencil mark at the top of the head. A read-out beside the chart is empty: "___ feet ___ inches".
- Instruction line: "Drag the mark to 5 feet 2 inches."
- The child is invited to drag the pencil mark up the chart.
2. Scene and Objects
- Chart: about 80% of the stage height. Foot marks are long and numbered; inch marks are short; 12 inch marks stand between two foot marks. The pencil mark snaps to each inch mark. The child figure stretches or shrinks with the mark.
- Read-outs: two wheels, "feet" and "inches" (0 to 11), a box "in inches" and a small chip "in cm". A foot bracket: a bracket that covers 12 inch marks and snaps onto the chart.
- Class board (Activity 4 and Star 2): a small wooden board at the top of the stage with student cards, each with a "feet" and an "inches" wheel and a tick box. A gold crown chip.
- Inch ruler (Star 1): a ruler (photo) with a cm and mm scale on one edge and an inch scale on the other, and a draggable needle.
- Goal chip, for example "5 feet 2 inches is ___ inches". Pills: 1, 2, 3, 4, star, star.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag the pencil mark; turn a wheel with its arrows; tap "+1 foot" to peel a foot bracket of 12 inches off a long number of inches; drag the crown onto a student card; drag the needle on the ruler. A number pad takes the "in inches" answer.
- Bottom buttons: Hint, Check (becomes Next when done), Reset. Undo is a small back arrow; retry is free.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Drag the mark to 5 feet 2 inches." Chip: "5 feet 2 inches is ___ inches". Setup: the chart with the foot brackets shown; wheels set to 5 and 2 by the mark. Guess: before dragging, the child taps "7 inches", "52 inches" or "62 inches". The child drags the mark to 5 feet 2 inches. Result: the 12-inch brackets count 5 feet and 2 more inches: "5 feet 2 inches is 5 × 12 + 2 = 62 inches." Help: guided.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "The mark is at 45 inches. Read it in feet and inches." Chip: "45 inches is ___ feet ___ inches". Setup: a strip of 45 inch marks above the chart. Guess: "4 feet 5 inches", "3 feet 9 inches" or "3 feet 15 inches". The child taps "+1 foot" three times: three brackets of 12 inches peel off and 9 inches are left. Result: "3 × 12 = 36, and 45 − 36 = 9 inches left, so 3 feet 9 inches." Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "How many cm is 2 feet?" Chip: "2 feet is ___ cm". Setup: the mark at 2 feet, the cm scale on the right edge, no brackets. Guess: "24 cm", "60 cm" or "240 cm". The child reads the cm edge at the mark. Result: "1 foot is 30 cm, so 2 feet is 2 × 30 = 60 cm." Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Find the tallest. Change each height to inches." Chip: "Tallest of 3". Setup: three student cards "4 feet 1 inch", "3 feet 11 inches" and "4 feet 2 inches" with an empty "in inches" box each. Guess: the child taps the card they think is tallest. The child types the inches and drags the crown to the tallest. Result: "4 × 12 + 1 = 49, 3 × 12 + 11 = 47 and 4 × 12 + 2 = 50 inches. 50 is the most, so 4 feet 2 inches is the tallest." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1 (the book's question). Goal line: "Look at your ruler to see if inches are also marked on it. Find out how many cm and mm equal 1 inch." Chip: "1 inch is ___ cm ___ mm". Setup: the inch ruler with the needle at 0. Guess: the child taps "less than 2 cm" or "more than 2 cm". The child drags the needle to the 1 inch mark and turns the cm and mm wheels. Result: "The 1 inch mark falls after 2 cm and 5 small marks: 1 inch is 2 cm 5 mm, which is 25 mm. 12 × 25 = 300 mm, which is 30 cm, 1 foot." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2 (the book's question). Goal line: "Stand against a wall and mark your height. Measure the distance between the floor and the marked point in feet and inches. Similarly, other students in the class can also measure their heights. Find out who is the tallest student in your class. What is his or her height in feet and inches?" Chip: "Tallest student". Setup: three students stand against the chart with pencil marks, a class board with three cards. Practice values: first 4 feet 3 inches, second 4 feet 7 inches, third 4 feet 5 inches. Guess: the child taps the student who looks tallest. The child taps each student, turns the feet and inches wheels to the pencil mark, types each height in inches, drags the crown to the tallest and sets the wheels for the tallest height. Result: "4 × 12 + 3 = 51, 4 × 12 + 7 = 55 and 4 × 12 + 5 = 53 inches. 55 is the most, so the second student is the tallest, 4 feet 7 inches. Your answer may differ." An "Add a student" chip (up to 3 more) lets the child add real classmates with the wheels; the tallest is found the same way. Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Dragging the mark and counting the 12-inch brackets shows that every foot holds 12 inches, so feet and inches change to inches by multiplying the feet by 12 and adding the inches. Peeling off brackets shows the way back.
- The class board shows that to compare heights, change all of them to the same unit, inches.
- Rules in the child's words: 1 foot is 12 inches; feet and inches to inches: feet × 12, then add the inches; 1 inch is 2 cm 5 mm and 1 foot is 30 cm.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the mark or wheel and the goal chip turn green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick and Next unlocks. Confetti only on the end screen.
- Wrong (every case): red strip, a small shake, ONE friendly line; no score; try again.
- 1 foot as 10 inches (for example 5 feet 2 inches as 52 inches) -> "1 foot is 12 inches, not 10 inches. Count the inch marks between two foot marks." The inch marks pulse.
- Added feet and inches (7 inches) -> "You added the feet and the inches. 5 feet is 5 × 12 inches. Then add the 2 inches."
- 12 inches or more left (3 feet 15 inches) -> "12 inches make 1 foot. Change them to feet."
- Compared only the feet -> "Two students have 4 feet. Look at the inches too." The inch wheels pulse.
- 2 feet as "24 cm" -> "24 is the number of inches in 2 feet. 1 foot is 30 cm, so count in 30s."
- Wrong reading on the inch ruler -> "1 inch is a little more than 2 cm. Count the small marks after 2 cm." The cm marks pulse.
- Hints (3 levels): (1) "How many inches are in 1 foot? Count the inch marks between two foot marks." (2) a foot bracket covers 12 inch marks on the chart, numbered 1 to 12; (3) "Multiply the feet by 12 and add the inches to get inches. To change inches to feet and inches, take out the full 12s." and the mark snaps to the height.
- Edge cases: 0 inches (5 feet is 60 inches); 11 inches is still less than 1 foot; two heights with the same feet are compared by inches; the book's inch is 2 cm 5 mm, so 12 inches make exactly 30 cm.
7. Ending
- Star 1 is done when the wheels read 2 cm 5 mm; Star 2 when 55 inches, the second student and 4 feet 7 inches are right.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "1 foot is 12 inches." "To change feet and inches to inches, multiply the feet by 12 and add the inches." "1 inch is 2 cm 5 mm, and 1 foot is 30 cm." Think and talk: "Two students are both 4 feet tall. How can you tell who is taller?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Photos: wooden height chart on a cream wall; a ruler with a cm edge and an inch edge. Flat drawings: three students of different heights, Shikha. Code-drawn: marks, wheels, brackets, class board, crown, needle. Language: "feet" and "inches" written out in full.

content.text:
Worked example: Shikha's height is 4 feet 6 inches (practice values). How many inches is that? Then change 30 inches into feet and inches.
1. 1 foot = 12 inches, so multiply the feet by 12.
2. 4 feet = 4 × 12 = 48 inches.

content.text:
1. Each row, each column and each $2 \times 2$ box has $+$, $-$, $\times$ and $\div$ once. Start with a box that has only one choice.
2. Row $1$ has $\div$ and $+$, so its other two boxes are $-$ and $\times$ . Column $2$ already has $\times$ in row $2$, so the top second box is $-$ and the top third box is $\times$ .
[Image: Try This: Ans1: solution]
3. Row $4$ needs $\div$ , $+$ and $\times$ in its first three boxes. Column $3$ already has $\times$ and $+$, so the bottom third box is $\div$ . Column $2$ already has $-$ and $\times$ , so the bottom second box is $+$, and the bottom first box is $\times$ .
4. Row $2$ needs $\div$ , $+$ and $-$ in its other boxes. Column $4$ already has $+$ and $-$, so the right box of row $2$ is $\div$ . Column $3$ already has $\times$ , $+$ and $\div$ , so the third box of row $2$ is $-$, and the first box is $+$.
5. Row $3$ needs $-$, $\div$ and $\times$ . Column $1$ already has $\div$ , $+$ and $\times$ , so the first box of row $3$ is $-$. Column $2$ already has $-$, $\times$ and $+$, so the second box is $\div$ , and the last box is $\times$ .
6. The completed grid: row $1 \div$ , $-$, $\times$ , $+$; row $2 +$, $\times$ , $-$, $\div$ ; row $3 -$, $\div$ , $+$, $\times$ ; row $4 \times$ , $+$, $\div$ , $-$.
7. Check: every row, every column and every $2 \times 2$ box has all four signs once.
Answer: Row $1$: $\div$ , $-$, $\times$ , $+$; row $2$: $+$, $\times$ , $-$, $\div$ ; row $3$: $-$, $\div$ , $+$, $\times$ ; row $4$: $\times$ , $+$, $\div$ , $-$
[Image: Try This: Ans1: solution (continued)]

topics.summary: The chapter's ideas in one walk along the measuring tape: the unit that fits, one length in two units, comparing and the difference, the kilometre and equal pieces, distance between stations, the millimetre, changing units, adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing lengths, the price of a length, estimating, feet and inches, and the sign puzzle.

content.text:
1. Predict first: you have walked along the whole measuring tape of the weaving centre. Can you say one idea from each stop, from the unit that fits to the sign puzzle? Read the lines below and tick each idea you remembered.
2. Choosing a unit: short things such as a pencil are measured in cm and long things such as a wall are measured in m, so the number sounds sensible.
3. One length, two names: 1 m = 100 cm. 3 m = 3 × 100 = 300 cm, and 450 cm = 4 m 50 cm.
4. Check: 5 m = 5 × 100 = 500 cm, so 480 cm is less than 5 m.
5. Comparing: change both lengths to the same unit, then compare. 4 m 3 cm = 403 cm, which is less than 430 cm.
6. Difference: the bigger length minus the smaller length in the same unit. 285 − 260 = 25 cm.
7. The kilometre: 1 km = 1,000 m, so 7 km = 7 × 1,000 = 7,000 m.
8. Equal pieces: a 2 km track with a flag after every 400 m needs 2,000 ÷ 400 = 5 flags.
9. Check: how many ropes of 125 m make 1 km? 1,000 ÷ 125 = 8 ropes.
10. Distance between two stations: subtract the two distances from the start. 615 − 340 = 275 km.
11. The millimetre: 1 cm = 10 mm, so 3 cm = 3 × 10 = 30 mm, and 4 cm 6 mm = 4 × 10 + 6 = 46 mm.
12. Changing units: from a bigger unit to a smaller unit multiply by 10, 100 or 1,000, and from a smaller unit to a bigger unit divide. 9 m = 9 × 100 = 900 cm and 4,000 m = 4,000 ÷ 1,000 = 4 km.
13. Check: write 7,305 cm in m and cm. 7,305 cm = 7,300 cm + 5 cm = 73 m 5 cm.
14. Adding: add like units and regroup. 2 km 700 m + 1 km 800 m = 4 km 500 m.
15. Subtracting: change both to the smaller unit, or regroup 1 m as 100 cm. 9 m − 3 m 40 cm = 5 m 60 cm.
16. Multiplying and dividing: break the length into two units and work on each. 12 × 2 m 40 cm = 28 m 80 cm, and 18 km 900 m divided by 3 is 6 km 300 m.
17. Price: 3 m of ribbon costs ₹90, so 1 m costs 90 ÷ 3 = ₹30.
18. Estimating: pick a reference you know, count how many times it fits, and say about. A wall as high as 2 doors of 2 m is about 4 m high.
19. Feet and inches: 1 foot = 12 inches. 4 feet 6 inches = 4 × 12 + 6 = 54 inches.
20. Sign puzzle: fill the box that has only one choice left, using its row and its column.

objectives.objective_text: Students choose cm or m for a length by asking how big the thing is and picking the unit that gives a sensible number.
Students change a length from m to cm and from cm to m and cm using 1 m = 100 cm.
Students choose the unit, m or cm, for six lengths, and name the same length in m and cm by filling in number lines side by side and matching lengths.
Students compare two lengths given in different units by changing both to the same unit and then comparing the numbers.
Students find how much longer one length is than another by changing both to one unit and subtracting, and find the length that doubles to a given length.

Students compare the length of rods with <, = and > by changing to one unit, and find the difference of two statue heights, the least and the largest differences, and the statue that doubles to the tallest.

objectives.strand_name: Far and Near: Kilometres, Millimetres and Changing Units
objectives.objective_text: Students change a distance between kilometres and metres using 1 km = 1,000 m, and say that kilo stands for thousand.

objectives.strand_name: Far and Near: Kilometres, Millimetres and Changing Units
objectives.objective_text: Students find how many equal ropes or stops fit along a distance by dividing the distance by the length of one piece, and say where each stop stands.

objectives.strand_name: Far and Near: Kilometres, Millimetres and Changing Units
objectives.objective_text: Students find how many ropes of a given length make 1 kilometre, and how many water stations, children and flags a 3 km race track needs, with their positions.

objectives.strand_name: Far and Near: Kilometres, Millimetres and Changing Units
objectives.objective_text: Students find the distance between two stations by subtracting their distances from the start of the route.

objectives.strand_name: Far and Near: Kilometres, Millimetres and Changing Units
objectives.objective_text: Students find the length of a train journey and the distance between two stations from a table of distances from the start, and say which two stations are farther apart.

objectives.strand_name: Far and Near: Kilometres, Millimetres and Changing Units
objectives.objective_text: Students explain that 1 cm is divided into 10 equal parts called millimetres, count the small marks, and change cm to mm using 1 cm = 10 mm.

objectives.strand_name: Far and Near: Kilometres, Millimetres and Changing Units
objectives.objective_text: Students read a length from a ruler in cm and mm and in mm only, and draw a line of a given length.

objectives.strand_name: Far and Near: Kilometres, Millimetres and Changing Units
objectives.objective_text: Students count the small marks between two cm marks on a ruler, measure the lines of a design in cm and mm, record the length of a sprout in mm, and draw lines of given lengths.

objectives.strand_name: Far and Near: Kilometres, Millimetres and Changing Units
objectives.objective_text: Students change lengths between mm and cm, cm and m, and m and km by multiplying or dividing by 10, 100 or 1,000.

objectives.strand_name: Far and Near: Kilometres, Millimetres and Changing Units
objectives.objective_text: Students write a length in one unit as a length in two units, and a length in two units as one number in the smaller unit, by splitting it.

objectives.strand_name: Far and Near: Kilometres, Millimetres and Changing Units
objectives.objective_text: Students fill in the numbers and the multipliers on three number lines side by side, and change lengths between mm, cm, m and km in fourteen conversions.
Students add two lengths given in two units by adding like units, or by changing both to the smaller unit and adding.
Students subtract one length from another by changing both to the smaller unit or by regrouping a bigger unit into the smaller one.
Students add and subtract lengths given in two units in the book's examples and word problems, and find the bigger of two lengths and their difference.
Students multiply a length given in m and cm by a whole number by multiplying the m and the cm separately and regrouping.
Students divide a length given in km and m by a whole number by dividing each unit part, or by changing it to the smaller unit.
Students find the price of 1 m from the price of a longer piece and use it to find the cost of a given length and the length for a given cost.
Students find the cloth for many shirts, the price of 1 m, the thread and its cost for a border, and share a road into equal days to find the length laid each day.
Students estimate a height or a depth by choosing a reference length and counting how many times it fits.
Students estimate the height of a building, the height of a tree and the depth of a well or pool, and say which reference length they used.
Students change a height between feet and inches and inches using 1 foot = 12 inches, and say that 1 inch is 2 cm 5 mm.
Students find how many cm and mm make 1 inch, and write the heights of students in feet and inches and find the tallest.
Students fill a small grid with three signs so that no sign repeats in a row or a column, using the clues one at a time.
Students fill the book's 4 by 4 grid with the signs +, −, × and ÷ so that no sign repeats in any row, column or 2 × 2 box.

video_coverage.book_item: Book item: Identify the appropriate units for measuring each of the following. Write m or cm after each number. (a): the height of India Gate is 42 ___; (b): the length of a handkerchief is 40 ___; (c): the depth of a well is 50 ___; (d): the length of a mobile phone is 13 ___; (e): the length of an elephant's trunk is 2 ___; (f): the distance between two buttons on a shirt is 5 ___.

Book item: Shikha and Sonu are measuring the lengths of saris and stoles in the village weaving centre. You can take help of the double number line below. Fill in the blanks. Top line: 100 cm, ___ cm, 400 cm, 500 cm, 700 cm. Bottom line: 1 m, 2 m, ___ m, ___ m, ___ m.

Book item: Shikha and Sonu are measuring the lengths of saris and stoles in the village weaving centre. Find which measures represent the same sari or stole. First list: 204 cm, 540 cm, 750 cm, 240 cm, 404 cm. Second list: 5 m 40 cm, 2 m 204 cm, 2 m 4 cm, 2 m 40 cm, 6 m 150 cm.

Book item: Ritika is comparing the lengths of different rods. Compare them using <, =, > signs. (a): 456 cm ___ 5 m; (b): 55 cm + 200 cm ___ 200 cm + 54 cm; (c): 6 m 5 cm ___ 6 m 50 cm; (d): 2 m 150 cm ___ 3 m 50 cm; (e): 238 cm ___ 138 cm + 1 m.
Book item: Look at the picture of some of the world's tallest statues. What is the difference between the height of the tallest statue in the world and the Statue of Liberty?
Book item: Look at the picture of some of the world's tallest statues. Identify the statues whose heights have the least difference.
Book item: Look at the picture of some of the world's tallest statues. Identify the statues whose heights have the largest difference.
Book item: Look at the picture of some of the world's tallest statues. The height of which statue will be equal to the height of the Statue of Unity, if it is doubled?

Book item: Measure 100 m and 200 m on your school playground, or any other place in and around your school, using a long tape. Mark these points and draw a straight line. Walk on the lines and count the number of steps. Use this relationship between the number of steps taken and distance walked to find distances around you for at least 3 locations. Wherever possible, walk and find the number of steps. Otherwise, find the distance and estimate the number of steps. (a): Identify and write the locations that are the nearest and the farthest from your home. (b): Write the distances obtained above in increasing order. (c): Name a location that is equal to or more than 1,000 m from your home.

Book item: Ropes of different lengths are used to make 1 km. Find how many ropes of each length are needed to make 1 km. A rope of 1,000 m: 1 rope. (a): a rope of 100 m: ___ ropes; (b): a rope of 10 m: ___ ropes; (c): a rope of 200 m: ___ ropes; (d): a rope of 500 m: ___ ropes; (e): a rope of 250 m: ___ ropes.

Book item: Sheena and Jennifer are helping to organise a 3 km race. Help them with the arrangements for the race. Water stations are to be arranged after every 500 m. How many water stations must be set up? At what positions from the starting point will these water stations be placed?

Book item: Sheena and Jennifer are helping to organise a 3 km race. Children need to stand at an interval of 300 m to direct the runners. How many children are needed? At what positions from the starting point will the children be standing?
Book item: Sheena and Jennifer are helping to organise a 3 km race. Red and blue flags are to be placed alternately at every 50 m. How many red and blue flags are needed till the finish line?

Book item: The longest train journey in India is by The Vivek Express which runs from Dibrugarh in Assam to Kanniyakumari in Tamil Nadu. Look at the stations on the route shown in the table and answer. The total length of the route from Dibrugarh to Kanniyakumari is ___ km.
Book item: Look at the table of stations on the route of The Vivek Express from Dibrugarh. The distance between Vijayawada and Jalpaiguri Road is ___ km.
Book item: Look at the table of stations on the route of The Vivek Express from Dibrugarh. The distance between Vijayawada and Visakhapatnam is ___ km.
Book item: Look at the table of stations on the route of The Vivek Express from Dibrugarh. Which two stations are farther apart, Guwahati and Dimapur or Bhubaneswar and Jalpaiguri Road?
Book item: Look at the table of stations on the route of The Vivek Express from Dibrugarh. What is the distance between Guwahati and Coimbatore JN?
Book item: Let us look at the scale. Do you notice the small marks between 1 cm and 2 cm? Count how many marks there are between 1 cm and 2 cm.

Book item: Measure the lines in the design and write their measurements in cm and mm. The design has eight lines, each with an empty box beside it. In this question they are numbered from the top of the picture to the bottom: (1): the upper left slanting side of the large diamond; (2): the top side of the inner rectangle; (3): the right side of the big outer shape; (4): the right side of the inner rectangle; (5): the upper left side of the small tilted shape; (6): the lower left side of the small tilted shape; (7): the lower left slanting side of the large diamond; (8): the bottom side of the big outer shape.

Book item: Soak some seeds of whole moong or black or white chana overnight. Next morning, take them out and wrap them in a moist cloth to sprout them. Over the next 4 days, take out one seed each day and measure the length of sprout. For ease of measurement, you can either place the seed on a paper and mark the length of the sprout, or use a thread to find its length. Fill in the table: the length of the sprout in mm on Day 1, Day 2, Day 3 and Day 4.
Book item: Draw lines of the following lengths in your notebook using a scale. (a): 5 cm 5 mm; (b): 3 cm 6 mm; (c): 8 cm 3 mm; (d): 36 mm; (e): 67 mm.

Book item: Fill in the blanks appropriately in the double number line. Top line: 1 cm, 7 cm, 15 cm, ___ cm, ___ cm, ___ cm, 50 cm. Bottom line: 10 mm, ___ mm, ___ mm, 250 mm, 320 mm, 450 mm, ___ m. Fill in the two boxes ×___ as well: the arrow on the top line is ×7 and the arrow from the top line to the bottom line is ×10.

Book item: Fill in the blanks appropriately in the double number line. Top line: 1 m, 4 m, 10 m, ___ m, ___ m, ___ m, 21 m. Bottom line: ___ cm, ___ cm, ___ cm, 1,200 cm, 1,400 cm, 1,700 cm, ___ cm. Fill in the two boxes ×___ as well: the arrow on the top line is ×4 and the arrow from the top line to the bottom line is ×100.

Book item: Fill in the blanks appropriately in the double number line. Top line: 1 km, 9 km, 25 km, ___ km, ___ km, ___ km, 82 km. Bottom line: 1,000 m, ___ m, ___ m, 41,000 m, 55,000 m, 67,000 m, ___ m. Fill in the two boxes ×___ as well: the arrow on the top line is ×9 and the arrow from the top line to the bottom line is ×1,000.
Book item: Use your understanding from above to fill in the blanks appropriately. (a): 4 cm 5 mm = ___ mm; (b): 89 mm = ___ cm ___ mm; (c): 234 cm = ___ mm; (d): 514 mm = ___ cm ___ mm.

Book item: Use your understanding from above to fill in the blanks appropriately. (e): 6 m 34 cm = ___ cm; (f): 20 m 12 cm = ___ cm; (g): 397 m = ___ cm; (h): 5,792 cm = ___ m ___ cm; (i): 9,108 cm = ___ m ___ cm.

Book item: Use your understanding from above to fill in the blanks appropriately. (j): 34 km = ___ m; (k): 6,870 m = ___ km ___ m; (l): 10,552 m = ___ km ___ m; (m): 29 km 30 m = ___ m; (n): 32 km 359 m = ___ m.
Book item: Saji saw on his smartphone that he walked 3 km 450 m in the morning and another 4 km 650 m in the evening. How much did he walk in the whole day? How would you solve this problem?
Book item: Electricians are changing the cables in a house. They need 63 m of cable for this purpose. They used 16 m 75 cm cable in the first room. What is the length of the cable left?
Book item: Rani has two red coloured ribbon rolls, one of length 3 m 75 cm and another 2 m 25 cm long. How much ribbon does she have?
Book item: The distance from Bhopal to Sanchi is 48 km 700 m. Bhadbhada Ghat waterfall is on the way, and 17 km 900 m away from Bhopal. How far is Sanchi from the waterfall?

Book item: Gulmarg Gondola in Gulmarg, Kashmir is the second longest and second highest cable car in the world. It is divided into two sections. The first section covers 2 km 300 m and the second section covers 2 km 650 m. What is the total distance covered by the cable car?
Book item: Circle the bigger length and find the difference. (a): 11 mm and 1 cm; (b): 26 mm and 2 cm; (c): 20 cm and 201 mm; (d): 1,020 mm and 1 m.
Book item: Circle the bigger length and find the difference. (e): 2 m and 245 cm; (f): 5,678 m and 6 km; (g): 6 km 1,480 m and 7 km 479 m.
Book item: We need a 1 m 80 cm cloth to make a shirt for a 10 year old child. How much cloth will be needed to make shirts for 20 such children?
Book item: A shop sells cloth for making bags at ₹100 for 5 m. How much money is needed to buy a 1 m cloth?

Book item: Now, use the double number line to find the cost of the cloth or the length of cloth that we can buy at a particular cost. Top line: 5 m, 10 m, 20 m, 40 m, ___ m. Bottom line: ₹100, ₹___, ₹___, ₹___, ₹2000. Fill in the four boxes ×___ as well.

Book item: Anita is making an embroidery on the border of a sari. She needs a 1 m long thread to embroider a 50 cm sari. How much thread would she need for a 5 m sari border? A 1 m long thread costs ₹50. How much money will be needed to buy the thread?
Book item: A road 12 km 600 m long is being laid in a town. The workers lay an equal length of road each day, and complete the work in 6 days. How much road laying work is done on each day?
Book item: Estimate the following. Share your reasoning in class. The height of the tallest building in your neighbourhood. What did you use as a reference to estimate the height?
Book item: Estimate the following. Share your reasoning in class. The height of the tallest tree in your neighbourhood. What did you use as a reference?
Book item: Estimate the following. Share your reasoning in class. The depth of a well or swimming pool in your neighbourhood. How did you find out?
Book item: Look at your ruler to see if inches are also marked on it. Find out how many cm and mm equal 1 inch.

Book item: Stand against a wall and mark your height. Measure the distance between the floor and the marked point in feet and inches. Similarly, other students in the class can also measure their heights. Find out who is the tallest student in your class. What is his or her height in feet and inches?
Book item: Put an appropriate operation sign (+, −, ×, ÷) in the empty boxes of the grid such that each row and column and each 2 × 2 box does not repeat the sign.

chapter_approach.intro: The chapter takes place in a village weaving centre with a long measuring tape on the wall, and on the roads, rulers and walls around it. Saris, stoles, ropes, trains, sprouts and statues are the lengths. Measuring them shows which unit fits, how one length has two names, and how to compare, add, subtract, multiply and divide lengths. A short video explains each idea, and an interactive tool lets the student try it alone.

points.text: Every idea has one short concept video. The tool that follows is where the student explores, builds and checks the idea alone, with hints, retry and reset. Eight tools, each with its own purpose, follow the chapter's own plan.
points.title: Videos teach, tools explore

points.text: Each tool opens with a short recall of the video idea, then lets the student play and apply it, and ends with the chapter's own question, used exactly as the book gives it.
points.title: A tool in three steps

points.text: Every solved example, Let Us Do question and every answerable prompt of the book is its own short video with a step by step solution and a question picture and a solution picture, in a Questions topic that follows the idea it practises.
points.title: Every book question has its own video

points.text: Tapes, rulers, bars and double number lines carry each idea: equal marks, the length as the largest thing on screen, and the unit written beside every number.
points.title: The picture is the mathematics

points.text: Heights of statues, station distances, ropes, cloth prices and every question are the book's own. Any number the plan adds is a practice value and is said to be one.
points.title: Only the book's numbers
